articles.title: AI-Enhanced CTA Triage Improves Detection of Intracranial Vessel Occlusions in Routine Clinical Workflow.
CurConMix+: A Unified Spatio-Temporal Framework for Hierarchical Surgical Workflow Understanding.
articles.abstract: Surgical action triplet recognition models fine-grained surgical interactions as structured triplets of ⟨instrument, verb, target⟩, but remains challenging because of severe class imbalance, subtle visual ambiguity, and compositional dependencies among triplet components. Existing approaches typically address only a subset of these challenges. We present CurConMix+, a unified spatio-temporal framework for surgical action triplet recognition. Its spatial component, CurConMix, learns structured and discriminative action representations through curriculum-guided contrastive learning, hard-pair sampling, and feature-level mixup. Its temporal component, the Multi-Resolution Temporal Transformer (MRTT), learnably combines multi-resolution temporal features and balances spatial and temporal evidence. We also introduce LLS48, extending surgical triplet recognition beyond cholecystectomy through aligned step, task, and action annotations sampled across 48 complete laparoscopic left lateral sectionectomy videos. Standalone CurConMix+ models achieve up to 42.2% APIVT on CholecT45 and 58.4% on LLS48, while CurConMix+-Ens further reaches 43.4% and 59.0%, respectively. Across three matched spatial backbones, MRTT consistently improves action-level segmental coherence on both datasets. The action-triplet-supervised CurConMix representations also improve phase, step, and task recognition over matched high-level supervised baselines, demonstrating effective transfer from fine-grained actions to higher-level workflow understanding. The code and LLS48 dataset will be released to support reproducible research in hierarchical surgical workflow understanding.

Agentic Automation of BT-RADS Scoring Using an End-to-End System for Standardized Glioma Follow-up Assessment.
articles.abstract: The Brain Tumor Reporting and Data System (BT-RADS) standardizes posttreatment MRI response assessment in patients with diffuse gliomas but requires complex integration of imaging trends, medication effects, and radiation timing. An end-to-end multiagent large language model and convolutional neural network system for automated BTRADS classification was developed and evaluated. Five hundred nine consecutive posttreatment glioma MRI examinations (March 2017-July 2021) from a single center were retrospectively evaluated. An extractor agent identified clinical variables from notes using gpt-oss (OpenAI, 20-billion parameters). A scorer agent applied BTRADS decision logic integrating these with quantitative volumetrics. System accuracy was compared against initial assessments, using expert annotation as the reference standard. Four hundred ninety-two examinations were evaluable. Overall system accuracy was 76.0% (374/492) versus 57.5% (283/492) for initial assessments, an absolute difference of +18.5 percentage points (P < .001). Cohen kappa between the system and the reference standard was 0.71. The system achieved high sensitivity in context-dependent categories (BT-1b; 100%; BT-1a, 92.7%; BT-3a, 87.5%) and moderate sensitivity for threshold-dependent categories (BT-3c, 74.8%; BT-2, 69.2%; BT-4, 69.3%; BT-3b, 57.1%). The BT-4 positive predictive value was 92.9%. These results support further evaluation of this system as a clinical decision-support tool, with local open-weight inference preserving data privacy.

articles.title: TRAM-AI: A Framework for Transparency in Reporting of Medical Imaging Datasets for Artificial Intelligence Development.
articles.abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate TRAM-AI, a consensus-based checklist for verifying whether medical imaging datasets described as publicly accessible are functionally usable for AI development. Materials and Methods A modified Delphi study was conducted. A steering committee generated candidate checklist items through a targeted literature review. An international expert panel (n = 33) rated items on criticality and feasibility across two Delphi rounds. Consensus was defined as ≥ 75% agreement on both dimensions. The checklist was pilot-validated in 10 publicly available datasets. An advisory group of four experts from Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa evaluated cross-regional applicability. Results Of 16 candidate items, 14 were retained in the final checklist; one item was removed because of feasibility concerns, and another was merged with an existing item because of conceptual redundancy. All 14 final items achieved consensus for both criticality and feasibility. The final TRAM-AI checklist comprises 14 items across four domains: Dataset Access and Persistence (3 items), Technical Interoperability (4 items), Metadata and Reproducibility (4 items), and Ethical, Legal, and Maintenance considerations (3 items). In pilot validation, all items were applicable to all 10 datasets, compliance was 90% for trusted repository, de-dentification, and subject-level mapping, 10% for archive validation, and 30% for partition keys. All four advisory group members endorsed the checklist. Conclusion TRAM-AI provides a practical framework for verifying the functional accessibility of medical imaging datasets, complementing existing methodological reporting standards. Further evaluation and broader validation across diverse geographic settings are warranted. ©RSNA, 2026.

articles.title: Interpretable Deep Learning for Opportunistic Screening of Left Ventricular Dysfunction Screening Using Chest Radiographs.
articles.abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate a deep learning model (DLLV) for identifying reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) on chest radiographs (CXRs) and assess its potential as a prescreening tool for selective transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in health checkup populations. Materials and Methods Same-day CXR-TTE pairs obtained between January 2016 and September 2021 were retrospectively collected for model development. Counterfactual learning was applied to enhance model performance and interpretability. External testing included one tertiary referral center cohort and two health checkup cohorts. Discrimination was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), and DLLV-based prescreening was evaluated by estimated TTE reduction and missed-case burden. Results The development dataset included 24,674 patients (32,135 CXR-TTE pairs); external cohorts included 5440, 28,034, and 6085 patients (53-62% male). DLLV achieved an AUC of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.84, 0.88) for LVEF ≤ 40% in the tertiary referral cohort. In health checkup cohorts, AUCs were 0.92-0.97 for LVEF ≤ 40%, with AUPRCs of 0.04 in both cohorts, corresponding to 87-fold (95% CI: 16, 404) and 37-fold (95% CI: 3, 251) enrichment over baseline prevalence. Counterfactual reinforcement learning produced heatmaps with greater heart localization precision (P < .001 for all) and higher AUC for LVEF < 50% (P = .04). DLLV-based prescreening estimated TTE volume reductions up to 85% while identifying all 12 and 7 individuals with LVEF ≤ 40%. Conclusion DLLV identified reduced LVEF on CXRs across external test cohorts and showed potential as a prescreening tool for selective TTE in health checkup populations. ©RSNA, 2026.

articles.title: A dual-prompt framework combining spatial-mask priors and clinical-text conditioning for CT-only GTV delineation in esophageal cancer: A multicenter study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation is essential for esophageal cancer radiotherapy, but CT-only automatic delineation remains difficult because of indistinct tumor boundaries. PURPOSE: This study aimed to develop and validate a two-stage dual-prompt framework combining a spatial-mask prior with LLaMA3-encoded clinical-text conditioning for primary esophageal GTV delineation. METHODS: This multicenter study included 857 patients: 500 for development, 125 for internal validation, 50 for ablation analysis, and 182 for external validation. The proposed framework consists of two stages: (1) a CT-based automatic segmentation network generating an initial GTV as a spatial mask prompt, and (2) a refinement network that jointly incorporates spatial mask prompt and LLaMA3-encoded clinical text prompt derived from structured clinical information. Performance was evaluated using overlap, surface distance, and volumetric metrics, and compared with multiple state-of-the-art deep learning models. Ablation and radiomics analyses assessed component contributions and downstream consistency. RESULTS: In internal validation, the framework achieved a DSC of 80.32 ± 6.65%, an HD95 of 11.42 ± 8.90 mm, and an absolute volume difference of 9.99 ± 10.49 mL; all Holm-adjusted p values were <0.001 versus the comparison models. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the external cohorts. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the two external cohorts, respectively. In external cohort A, ContextUNETR showed a lower mean HD95 than the proposed model (10.93 ± 8.03 vs. 13.44 ± 18.90 mm), although the paired difference was not statistically significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.906). Compared with the direct Stage-1 output, the complete framework consistently improved overlap, boundary-distance, and volumetric-agreement metrics across the internal and both external validation cohorts (all adjusted p < 0.001). LLaMA3 encoding improved DSC versus an MLP using the same variables (adjusted p = 0.009), whereas ASSD did not differ significantly. Automatic and manual GTVs showed high radiomic concordance and comparable prognostic performance. CONCLUSION: The framework improved overlap and volumetric agreement for CT-only primary esophageal GTV delineation across multicenter validation cohorts, although boundary-distance performance varied across external cohorts.

articles.title: ESR Bridges: high-risk steatotic liver disease: new developments in non-invasive tests and treatment-a multidisciplinary view.
ACR lung-RADS: updates and future directions.
articles.abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and low-dose CT (LDCT) screening has been shown to significantly reduce lung cancer deaths in high-risk populations. The American College of Radiology (ACR) introduced the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) in 2014 to standardize the reporting and management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules. Since its inception, Lung-RADS has undergone iterative updates reflecting advances in evidence, clinical practice, and the expanding scope of lung cancer screening. This review summarizes the major updates to Lung-RADS, highlights areas of active discussion within the Lung-RADS Committee, and outlines future research directions. Key topics include the ongoing evaluation of volumetric versus diameter-based nodule measurement, the management of subsolid nodules and the balance between surveillance and intervention, the implementation of Category 0 for infectious or inflammatory findings, clarification of juxtapleural nodule classification, the approach to incidental findings, and the development of a Lung-RADS Atlas. Future directions address the integration of risk-based and category-based assessment approaches, the role of artificial intelligence and deep learning in nodule stratification, the potential incorporation of incidental nodules into Lung-RADS, and the prospect of international harmonization for lung cancer screening reporting and management. Lung-RADS has become an essential reporting and quality tool for lung cancer screening in the United States and increasingly worldwide. Continued refinement, guided by emerging evidence, multidisciplinary collaboration, and technological innovation, will be critical to advancing precision screening strategies and reducing the global burden of lung cancer.Clinical trial numberNot applicable.

articles.title: Reporting of Fairness and Equity in Studies of Regulator-cleared Commercial AI for Acute Stroke CT: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Commercial artificial intelligence (AI) tools cleared by regulators now triage acute stroke on computed tomography (CT) scans across health systems whose patients differ in age, sex, race, socioeconomic status, and imaging hardware. It is unknown whether studies of these tools report how performance varies across such groups. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We systematically reviewed English-language studies of commercial, regulator-cleared AI tools for adult acute stroke CT tasks. PubMed, Scopus, and PubMed Central were searched from January 1, 2018, through June 2, 2026, and Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore were searched on September 14, 2026, for records published from 2018 onward; the searches were supplemented by a backward-reference and forward-citation audit. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Eight prespecified reporting items informed by CLAIM 2024, TRIPOD+AI, and evidence on algorithmic bias were scored as reported, partial, or not reported. The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261403480). RESULTS: Thirteen studies covering nine vendors and four CT tasks met the eligibility criteria. Only one study reported sociodemographic subgroup performance. It found lower positive predictive value for female patients than for male patients (67.3% vs. 72.7%; p = 0.02) and for Black patients than for non-Black patients (66.7% vs. 73.2%; p = 0.005). Performance by site, scanner, or protocol was reported in one other study. No included peer-reviewed study described the demographic composition of the tool's training data, and four studies acknowledged a potential bias or data gap without measuring it. CONCLUSION: Subgroup performance was rarely reported in the included peer-reviewed evaluations. The finding of positive predictive value differences in one study is insufficient to characterize fairness across products. Missing subgroup and training-population reporting limits assessment of fairness, but does not establish that the evaluated systems are inequitable.

articles.title: How to plan and deliver lung cancer reirradiation: A consensus approach from the ESTRO reirradiation and lung focus groups and ReCOG.
articles.abstract: Lung reirradiation is seeing increased use, yet the evidence base guiding its practice remains limited despite significant technological advances. This paper provides a consensus approach addressing the technical factors underpinning clinical decision-making. It aims to answer the central question: how can clinical teams implement a safe, reproducible, and technically robust workflow for high-dose lung reirradiation? The recommendations are developed by an expert panel of radiation oncologists, medical physicists, and radiation therapists (RTT) from 14 European, American, and Canadian centres, synthesizing a broad range of clinical perspectives. The scope of this work/manuscript is to provide a structured, practical workflow applicable across diverse clinical settings. Using a clinical case, the manuscript demonstrates key conceptual principles, such as the rationale for advanced dose accumulation and the impact of anatomical changes during treatment, with clear, stepwise guidance to support consistent implementation and informed clinical judgement. Key recommended steps include retrieval of prior treatment data; consideration of prior positioning and motion management; and equieffective dose accumulation using deformable image registration or organ-at-risk (OAR)-focused rigid registration. Treatment planning should explicitly incorporate prior dose while balancing target coverage against OAR limits. Daily online volumetric image guidance is central to evaluating both bony and soft-tissue anatomy, enabling setup adjustments to protect critical structures approaching tolerance. Clear documentation and multidisciplinary communication are integral throughout. This consensus approach is intended to support both centres that aim to establish reirradiation practice and experienced teams seeking to harmonize best practices.

Musculoskeletal shear-wave elastography in the paediatric population: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: In the literature, shear-wave elastography (SWE) is most often described for evaluating the elasticity of internal organs; nevertheless, it has also been increasingly used to assess the musculoskeletal system. In clinical and research settings, changes in the mechanical properties of musculoskeletal tissues can be observed in conditions related to overuse, sports injuries, congenital anomalies, neurological disorders, and other musculoskeletal conditions. SWE enables the assessment of these changes and may facilitate monitoring of disease-related alterations, therapeutic effects, and adaptations associated with physical training. The aim of this systematic review was to identify and synthesize all studies using SWE to assess the musculoskeletal system in the paediatric population. A total of 67 studies involving 2,558 children aged 1 day to 18 years were included. SWE was applied to a wide range of musculoskeletal structures and clinical populations, with substantial heterogeneity in study designs, ultrasound systems, measurement protocols, anatomical positioning, and reported outcomes. Twenty two studies assessed the reliability of SWE measurements, with reliability varying according to the examined structure and measurement conditions. Due to the substantial methodological and clinical heterogeneity of the included studies, a quantitative meta-analysis was not performed. Overall, the available evidence demonstrates a broad range of potential applications of SWE in paediatric musculoskeletal assessment, while also highlighting the need for greater methodological standardization and further research to establish robust reference values and clinically applicable protocols.

articles.title: Diffusion-Relaxation Correlation Spectroscopic MRI in Adult Gliomas: Spectral Heterogeneity and Associations With Histomolecular Features.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Preoperative MRI characterization of glioma histomolecular features is limited by intratumoral heterogeneity and the scalar nature of conventional diffusion and relaxation metrics. PURPOSE: To characterize glioma heterogeneity using diffusion-relaxation correlation spectroscopic imaging (DR-CSI) and evaluate associations with glioma grade, isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status, and Ki-67 index. STUDY TYPE: Prospective. POPULATION: Fifty Three treatment-naïve adults with histopathologically confirmed gliomas (mean age, 49.0 ± 13.9 years; 34 men). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3 T; multi-b, multi-TE diffusion-relaxation spin-echo echo-planar imaging sequence. ASSESSMENT: Voxelwise D-T2 spectra were reconstructed from multi-b-value, multi-echo-time data and clustered into seven spectral subregions (V1-V7). Spectral fractions and conventional metrics were normalized to normal-appearing white matter (NAWM): nV1-nV7, nADC1, and nT21 were obtained from the entire non-necrotic tumor, whereas nADC2 and nT22 were obtained from enhancing tumor (ET) in substantially enhancing lesions or non-enhancing tumor (NET) in lesions with little or no enhancement. Associations of these metrics with glioma grade (high or low), Ki-67 index, and IDH status (wild type or mutant) were investigated. STATISTICAL TESTS: Mann-Whitney U test, Spearman rank correlation coefficient (ρ), logistic regression, likelihood ratio testing, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, bootstrapped area under ROC curve (AUC). SIGNIFICANCE: p < 0.05. RESULTS: DR-CSI showed distinct D-T2 spectral patterns across ET, NET, necrosis/cystic change, and NAWM. nV3 significantly correlated with Ki-67 index (ρ = 0.401) and remained significantly associated with high-grade status after age adjustment (odds ratio [OR] per standard deviation [SD] increase = 6.020). nV5 was significantly associated with IDH-mutant status after age adjustment (OR per SD increase, 10.980). Including nV3 in addition to age significantly improved grade model fit (bootstrap-corrected AUC, 0.805 vs. 0.709). Including nADC2 and nV5 in addition to age significantly improved IDH model fit over age alone (bootstrap-corrected AUC, 0.953 vs. 0.877). DATA CONCLUSION: DR-CSI characterized D-T2 compartment spectral heterogeneity in gliomas, and DR-CSI metrics were associated with grade, Ki-67 index, and IDH status. These findings support DR-CSI as a composition-sensitive MRI approach for glioma heterogeneity assessment. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 2.

articles.title: Accuracy of Large Language Model Chatbots in Retrieving MRI Safety Conditions for Medical Implants.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Retrieving MRI safety conditions for implanted devices is increasingly complex and time-consuming. PURPOSE: To evaluate the accuracy of internet-enabled large language model (LLM) chatbots in retrieving implant-specific MRI safety conditions, using manufacturer documentation as the reference standard. STUDY TYPE: Prospective comparative evaluation in a constructed device cohort, followed by a retrospective clinical pilot. POPULATION: Fifty purposively selected device configurations and 20 patients (10 with cardiac and 10 with noncardiac devices) referred to the MRI Safety Committee. FIELD STRENGTH: No field-strength or sequence restrictions. ASSESSMENT: Standardized single-shot prompts requested eight parameters from ChatGPT-5.0, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5: MRI safety label, field strengths, eligible regions/centering, transmit-coil restrictions, RF exposure limits, maximum spatial gradient, maximum gradient slew rate, and scan duration. Two radiologists (10 and 25 years' experience) and an MRI technologist (32 years) independently scored 1200 parameter-level outputs against manufacturer Instructions for use and technical manuals using a 5-point scale (5, fully correct; 1, substantively incorrect or fabricated); scores of 4-5 indicated accuracy. In the pilot, 160 outputs from ChatGPT-5.6, a newer version of the best-performing chatbot, were scored identically. STATISTICAL TESTS: Intraclass correlation coefficient; Gwet's first-order agreement coefficient (AC1); Friedman test; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; device-clustered bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs); two-sided significance threshold, p < 0.05. RESULTS: Mean ordinal scores were 4.76 (ChatGPT), 4.20 (Gemini), and 4.17 (Claude); ChatGPT scored significantly higher. Respective pooled parameter-level accuracies were 0.94 (95% CI, 0.89-0.98), 0.79 (0.71-0.86), and 0.78 (0.69-0.87). Pilot accuracy with ChatGPT-5.6 was 0.98 (95% CI, 0.94-1.00). DATA CONCLUSION: Internet-enabled LLM chatbots correctly retrieved up to 94% of MRI safety parameters in the constructed cohort and 98% in the clinical pilot. Errors occurred even with the best-performing chatbot, requiring direct verification against current manufacturer documentation before clinical use. EVIDENCE LEVEL: Stage 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 2.

articles.title: Multi-Parametric Phase-Cycled Balanced Steady-State Free Precession Brain Tissue Characterization in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Time-efficient phase-cycled balanced steady-state free precession (pc-bSSFP) imaging is a novel microstructure- and myelin-sensitive approach for multi-parametric brain tissue characterization not yet evaluated in demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS). PURPOSE: To evaluate quantitative relaxometry metrics in white matter (WM) and gray matter (GM) of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) and healthy control (HC) cohorts using a multi-parametric pc-bSSFP framework. STUDY TYPE: Prospective and retrospective, observational. POPULATION: Twenty RRMS patients (34.5 ± 5.9 years, female 15/20) and 10 HC subjects (33.4 ± 6.9 years, female 5/10). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3 T; T1-weighted magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo, T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, pc-bSSFP, B1 + mapping, single-shot spin-echo echo-planar-imaging diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). ASSESSMENT: R1, R2, and the bSSFP asymmetry index (AI) were compared between RRMS and HC across selected WM and GM regions of interest (ROIs). DTI-derived fiber-to-field angle, number of fiber orientations, and fractional anisotropy were used for parameter anisotropy analysis. STATISTICAL TESTS: Linear mixed-effects models tested group, ROI, and group-by-ROI effects for each metric. Anisotropy differences between cohorts were assessed with two-sided t-tests. ROI and anisotropy tests employed false discovery rate correction with significance set at pcorr < 0.05. RESULTS: Significant group, ROI, and group-by-ROI effects were found for R1 (β = -0.16) and R2 (β = -2.84). The ROI effect was significant for AI while the group (p = 0.450) and group-by-ROI (p = 0.747) effects were non-significant. Age and sex covariates did not reach significance (Age: p = [0.563, 0.705, 0.591], Gender: p = [0.839, 0.822, 0.179], for [R1, R2, AI]). Fourteen of 16 ROIs showed significantly lower R1 and R2 (d = -4.25 to -0.85) in RRMS than HC. All ROIs remained non-significant for AI. R2 (pcorr ≥ 0.055) and AI (pcorr ≥ 0.108) anisotropy comparison between RRMS and HC groups did not reach significance. DATA CONCLUSION: Phase-cycled bSSFP relaxometry showed WM-predominant differences in RRMS, with additional whole-brain assessment including gray matter. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 1.

articles.title: Quantitative UTE MRI Differences in the Meniscus Following ACL Reconstruction: A Prospective Cohort Study Using 3D Ultrashort Echo Time Adiabatic T1rho and Magnetization Transfer Imaging.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: ACLR is associated with altered joint loading and increased risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Conventional MRI has limited sensitivity to early meniscal differences because of short-T2 signal decay and magic-angle effects. PURPOSE: To evaluate whether 3D ultrashort echo time imaging-based adiabatic T1rho (UTE-Adiab-T1rho) and ultrashort echo time imaging-based macromolecular fraction (UTE-MMF) identify regional quantitative MRI differences after ACLR. STUDY TYPE: Prospective longitudinal cohort study. POPULATION: 30 control scans, 19 ACLR scans at 6-12 months, and 13 ACLR scans at 12+ months were analyzed. Mean ages were 34.5, 34.5, and 37.2 years; female/male counts were 15/15, 9/10, and 8/5. FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: Participants underwent 3-T knee MRI with 3D fat-saturated UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE magnetization transfer sequences. ASSESSMENT: UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF maps were generated with single-component exponential and two-pool magnetization transfer models. Values were extracted from four meniscal regions of interest by a blinded reader, with blinded redelineation in a subset. Patient-reported outcomes included International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index scores. STATISTICAL TESTS: Linear mixed-effects models accounted for repeated observations. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction was applied. RESULTS: UTE-Adiab-T1rho showed significant group (q = 0.001) and region (q < 0.001) effects. Compared with controls, UTE-Adiab-T1rho was higher in LAM at 6-12 months (+5.60 ms; q = 0.035) and 12+ months (+7.09 ms; q = 0.028), and in LPM at 12+ months (+6.35 ms; q = 0.035). UTE-MMF showed significant group (q = 0.041) and region (q < 0.001) effects. LPM UTE-MMF was lower than controls at 6-12 months (-3.56 percentage points; q = 0.028) and 12+ months (-3.10 percentage points; q = 0.049). No 6-12 versus 12+ month MRI or PROM contrast survived FDR correction. MRI-PROM associations were not FDR-significant (all q ≥ 0.383). DATA CONCLUSION: UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF mapping identified regional MRI differences after ACLR. Pairwise differences were concentrated in lateral regions, but corrected group-by-region interactions were not significant. PROMs were worse after ACLR but did not differ between postoperative windows after correction. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY STAGE: 2.

articles.title: Clinical impact of PSMA PET/CT on the management of biochemical recurrence in prostate cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ga-68 prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) improves lesion detection in patients with biochemical recurrence (BCR) of prostate cancer. However, real-world evidence linking imaging-driven management changes to early biochemical outcomes remains limited, particularly in Korean populations. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of Ga-68 PSMA PET/CT on clinical management and its association with early biochemical response. METHODS: This study included retrospectively registered 75 patients who underwent Ga-68 PSMA PET/CT for suspected BCR after radical prostatectomy between September 2022 and February 2024. Intended management at referral and final management after PET were compared. Biochemical outcomes were assessed based on follow-up prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels. RESULTS: Seventy-five patients were analyzed (median age, 71 years; median PSA level, 0.30 ng/mL). PSMA PET/CT demonstrated positive findings in 28 patients (37.3%), including equivocal finding. Overall, intended management was changed in 19 patients (25.3%) following PET/CT. At after 2 years of follow-up, 49 patients achieved PSA ≤ 0.20 ng/mL, and 36 achieved PSA ≤ 0.03 ng/mL. CONCLUSIONS: In prostate cancer patients with suspected BCR, Ga-68 PSMA PET/CT led to clinically meaningful changes in management and influenced treatment selection in a Korean cohort. Larger prospective studies are warranted to further define its incremental clinical value.

articles.title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer in Transrectal Ultrasound.
articles.abstract: Diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) using transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) remains a challenging task due to limited image contrast and the subtle appearance of malignant lesions. In this study, we propose a novel hybrid framework that integrates multi-modality and multi-task learning for csPCa classification from TRUS data. The framework leverages complementary information from B-mode and strain elastography (SE) imaging via a dual-stream encoder, enhanced by cross-modal attention gate (CMAG) modules at each level. These CMAG modules first adaptively integrate cross-modal features and then employ a gating mechanism to regulate the flow of cross-modal context into each modality-specific stream. To mitigate the scarcity of segmentation annotations, we introduce a multi-scale prototype-guided learning (MSPL) strategy, which propagates supervision signals from a small set of labeled samples to unlabeled ones by leveraging learned prototypes across multiple feature scales. This design allows the task-shared encoder to benefit from structural cues captured by the segmentation branch, even with minimal voxel-level supervision. Additionally, a context-aware multi-scale classifier (CMSC) aggregates hierarchical decoder features to further exploit the synergy between classification and segmentation tasks. The proposed method is evaluated on an in-house dataset containing 612 subjects who underwent prostate biopsy and attains favorable performance in identifying csPCa with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.86. Extensive comparative and ablation results further highlight the efficacy of incorporating cross-modal interaction, prototype-guided learning, and context-aware classification for accurate and annotation-efficient csPCa diagnosis. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/mock1ngbrd/ProstateMMTNet .

articles.title: Clinical CT Data Infrastructure Provides Partial Support for an Operational Ontology for Radiology.
articles.abstract: Medical imaging data are increasingly used beyond patient care to support research, quality assessment, and artificial intelligence development. These applications require imaging examinations to be represented in ways that enable consistent aggregation across clinical operations to ensure reliable interpretation. In prior work, we introduced an ontology framework, the Operational Ontology for Radiology (OOR), designed to represent the radiology imaging workflow for computed tomography (CT) examinations through entities and relationships. This investigation evaluates the extent to which existing clinical imaging infrastructure can support the implementation of this framework. Using OOR, 156 data properties representing components of the imaging workflow were assessed within the clinical imaging environment at one academic medical center. Each property was classified according to its availability in institutional data systems into four categories: directly available and standardized, indirectly available and standardized, available but not standardized, or not readily available. The distribution of properties across these categories was quantified overall and across ontology classes. Among the evaluated properties, 48.1% were directly available in structured form, 7.1% were indirectly available and standardized, 33.3% required standardization, and 11.5% were not readily available in the systems. Technical acquisition parameters, device information, and patient attributes were most frequently available, while elements related to imaging tasks, contextual workflow attributes, and certain series-level descriptors required standardization or structured representation. These findings demonstrate that a portion of OOR can be supported using clinical data infrastructures, while also identifying areas where improved standardization and structured data representation are needed to enable large-scale analysis of clinical imaging data.

articles.title: Toward Verifiable Medical Imaging World Models: An Engineering Framework for Evaluating Simulation Fidelity, Roll-Out Stability, and Clinical Plausibility.
articles.abstract: Medical world models simulate how a patient's imaged state evolves over time and, in some systems, under clinical interventions. Their value comes from multi-step, action-conditioned roll-outs, yet evaluation is still dominated by perceptual or single-step metrics. We treat assessment of these models as a verification problem, distinct from later evidence of clinical benefit, and organize it around three axes. Simulation fidelity asks whether predicted states are correct at the level claimed by the model. Roll-out stability asks whether that correctness is maintained over multiple steps; we summarize this using an effective planning horizon, defined as the last step before a stated loss quantile first exceeds a clinical tolerance under the observed action policy. Clinical plausibility and reliability ask whether simulated responses are counterfactually consistent, calibrated, and adequate across patient subgroups. We also propose a claim-proportionate reporting standard and a reproducible procedure for estimating the horizon from retrospective data. Applying the framework to a purposively selected sample of nine imaging world models, we find that reported evidence is uneven across capability tiers. Under the proposed standard, every model claiming action-conditioned prediction or above omits at least one applicable item: none reports an explicit counterfactual-consistency check or a clinically meaningful subgroup analysis of the type specified in Item 7, and none reports an effective planning horizon at a stated clinical tolerance. Because the effective planning horizon is estimated on-policy, it should not be interpreted as evidence of off-policy counterfactual reliability.

articles.title: TRACE-CLDN: An Integrated Computational Pathology Framework for Tumor-Restricted Quantification of CLDN18.2 Expression Burden from H&E Whole-Slide Images in Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma.
articles.abstract: Claudin-18.2 (CLDN18.2) is a membrane-associated biomarker with emerging translational relevance in biliary tract cancers. In intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC), whole-slide image (WSI)-level assessment is complicated by abundant stroma, dispersed tumor glands, non-neoplastic epithelial structures, and heterogeneous membranous staining. We developed TRACE-CLDN (Tumor-Restricted Analysis for Computational Estimation of CLDN18.2), an integrated computational pathology framework for tumor-restricted quantification of CLDN18.2 expression burden from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) WSIs. This retrospective study included 135 ICC cases with paired H&E and CLDN18.2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) WSIs. After cross-modal registration, IHC-derived annotations were mapped to H&E images to generate patch-level training data. TRACE-CLDN integrates two independently trained H&E-based modules for tumor region identification and CLDN18.2 expression label prediction, followed by WSI-level tumor-restricted aggregation. Agreement with pathologist consensus was assessed in a 45-case pathologist-validation subset, and exploratory survival analysis was performed in the full cohort. ROC-AUCs were 0.9968 ± 0.0009 for tumor identification and 0.9633 ± 0.0174 for expression prediction. The TRACE-CLDN-derived Ratio showed strong agreement with pathologist assessment (Spearman ρ = 0.876; weighted κ = 0.767). In exploratory survival analysis, the log-rank P value was 0.010 and the concordance index was 0.668. TRACE-CLDN enables tumor-restricted, continuous assessment of CLDN18.2 expression burden from H&E WSIs, with strong agreement with pathologist assessment and an exploratory association with survival in ICC.

articles.title: Full-Cohort Organ Dose Assessment from Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening in the National Lung Screening Trial.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Organ-specific dose estimates are needed to characterize radiation exposure from repeated low-dose computed tomography (CT) lung cancer screening in the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). The objective was to estimate study-level doses and participant-level cumulative doses in the NLST CT screening cohort. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective dosimetry study included 25,051 NLST CT screening participants from the Lung Screening Study and American College of Radiology Imaging Network components after excluding participants with any examination lacking a valid manufacturer-appropriate tube current-time input. Image-series metadata were linked with age, sex, height, and weight, and then valid records were grouped into 69,601 study-level screening examinations. Organ absorbed doses and effective dose were calculated using the National Cancer Institute dosimetry system for Computed Tomography with sex- and body-size-specific adult phantoms. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was assessed with 50 stochastic simulations. RESULTS: Participants underwent a mean of 2.78 study-level screening examinations; the median study-level volume CT dose index was 3.30 mGy. Median (interquartile range) study-level lung, breast, heart wall, active marrow, and effective doses were 3.93 (3.13-4.96), 3.94 (3.14-5.04), 3.94 (3.14-5.01), and 1.26 (0.99-1.60) mGy, and 2.07 (1.65-2.59) mSv, respectively. Corresponding cumulative participant-level doses were 11.30 (8.89-14.50), 11.39 (9.01-14.75), 11.41 (8.93-14.66), and 3.63 (2.79-4.66) mGy, and 5.94 (4.69-7.64) mSv. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was greatest for thyroid dose (mean coefficient of variation, 21.1%) and low for in-field organs. CONCLUSION: Using NLST low-dose CT screening data, we estimated participant-level cumulative organ and effective doses and characterized variation across organs and body-size groups.

articles.title: Periprocedural Cardiac Hemodynamic Changes and Clinical Outcomes After Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: To characterize serial changes in cardiac structure and function before and after transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) using comprehensive echocardiographic assessment and to explore their clinical relevance. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 149 patients with decompensated cirrhosis who underwent TIPS between January 2018 and October 2024. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed preoperatively, within 5 days after TIPS, and at 3-6 months of follow-up. Additional echocardiographic parameters were assessed preoperatively and early after TIPS during hospitalization to further characterize periprocedural cardiac functional changes. Echocardiographic parameters were compared across time points using repeated-measures analysis or paired tests. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was used to examine associations with clinical outcomes. RESULTS: After TIPS, right atrial diameter and right ventricular end-diastolic diameter increased significantly (both P < 0.001), accompanied by a modest increase in pulmonary artery systolic pressure (P = 0.029), while left ventricular structure and systolic function showed no significant changes. The tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion/pulmonary artery systolic pressure ratio showed a numerical decrease early after TIPS, followed by partial recovery during follow-up, although the changes were not statistically significant. Among the additional echocardiographic parameters, color M-mode flow propagation velocity (Vp) increased significantly from 62.8 to 75.1 cm/s (P = 0.04), whereas E/A, E/e', and other diastolic parameters remained largely unchanged. During a median follow-up of 1057 days, one patient developed early postoperative heart failure. Survival and overt hepatic encephalopathy did not differ significantly among groups stratified by baseline E/A ratio. CONCLUSION: In patients with relatively preserved baseline cardiac function following appropriate pre-TIPS cardiovascular assessment, TIPS was associated predominantly with mild and transient right-sided cardiac changes, without significant deterioration in conventional left ventricular systolic function. The low incidence of clinically overt cardiac decompensation observed during follow-up suggests an acceptable cardiac risk profile in appropriately evaluated patients.

articles.title: Nurse-Led Gastric Preparation for Gas-Negative-Contrast Volume-Rendered Three-Dimensional Virtual Endoscopy-Like Gastric Imaging on Photon-Counting CT: A Prospective Randomized Clinical Study.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate nurse-led gastric preparation for photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT)-based gas-negative-contrast volume-rendered (gas-VRT) virtual endoscopic gastric imaging, focusing on effervescent powder dose, PCCT-related image-quality advantages, and water-assisted preparation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This single-center prospective randomized trial enrolled 120 patients undergoing contrast-enhanced abdominal CT. Participants were allocated into four groups (n = 30 each): PCCT-3g, PCCT-6g, energy-integrating detector (EID)-6g, and PCCT-3g+W. All gastric preparations followed standardized nurse training and a nurse-led five-step preparation protocol, including patient instruction, protocol-specific gastric preparation, breath-holding guidance, positioning, and scan-timing control. The primary endpoint was the gas-VRT virtual endoscopy-like imaging quality score. Secondary endpoints included intragastric gas/liquid volume, overall and antral gastric distension, gastric wall layer visibility, quantitative image metrics, patient tolerance, and adverse events. RESULTS: All patients finished examinations without severe adverse events. PCCT-6g achieved a larger intragastric gas volume than PCCT-3g, with an increase of 201.85 cm³, superior gastric distension and gas-VRT quality (all P < 0.001), accompanied by higher discomfort (numeric rating scale score, 0.63 ± 0.85 vs 0.07 ± 0.25). At an identical 6 g effervescent dose, PCCT and EID-CT yielded comparable distension and gas-VRT images; PCCT provided lower noise (5.37 ± 0.72 HU vs 10.90 ± 1.98 HU) and improved signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (12.56 ± 1.92 vs 5.08 ± 0.88), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) (18.89 ± 4.16 vs 4.97 ± 1.80), and wall layer visualization (all P < 0.001). Water supplementation increased intragastric liquid volume by 279.68 cm³ and antral distension score by 2.13 points in the PCCT-3g group, but failed to enhance gas-VRT quality. CONCLUSION: Nurse-led PCCT gastric preparation can be customized for different imaging objectives. Six grams of effervescent powder is preferable for gas-VRT virtual endoscopic imaging, while 3 g may be sufficient for routine gastric evaluation. Under the same 6 g preparation protocol, PCCT provided lower image noise, higher SNR/CNR, and clearer gastric wall layer visualization than EID-CT, suggesting platform-specific value beyond gastric distension alone. Water assistance may benefits antral cross-sectional assessment but did not improve gas-VRT imaging.

articles.title: Machine Learning Model Using Clinical and Contrast-Enhanced MRI Features Differentiates Cerebral Tuberculoma from Lung Cancer Brain Metastasis.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Cerebral tuberculomas (CTB) and lung cancer brain metastases (BM) frequently show overlapping appearances on conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) but require entirely different treatment strategies. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning model integrating clinical and contrast-enhanced MRI features to noninvasively differentiate these two entities. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The internal dataset (n = 188, 122 CTB, 66 BM) was split into training/validation (n = 131) and internal test (n = 57) sets. Feature selection (univariate and stepwise logistic regression) was performed only on the training and validation set, yielding four predictors. Machine learning classifiers were trained using these predictors with repeated 5-fold cross-validation. An external test set (n = 51, 26 CTB, 25 BM) from another hospital was used for independent validation. RESULTS: Multivariate logistic regression retained four independent predictors: age (OR = 1.046, 95%CI: 1.003-1.091, p = 0.036), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (odds ratios [OR] = 1.711, 95%confidence intervals [CI]: 1.235-2.370, p = 0.001), multiple lesions (OR = 0.080, 95%CI: 0.015-0.438, p = 0.004), and ring with mural nodule (OR = 11.289, 95%CI: 2.551-49.952, p = 0.001). The Gradient Boosting model built on these four features achieved the best performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.970 (95%CI: 0.925-0.998) on the internal test set and 0.957 (95%CI: 0.900-0.995) on the external test set. On the external test set, the model showed a sensitivity of 88.0% and a specificity of 92.3%. CONCLUSION: A Gradient Boosting model integrating age, CEA, multiple lesions, and ring with mural nodule effectively distinguishes CTB from BM with robust external test performance, providing a noninvasive tool to assist clinical decision-making.

articles.title: MRI Interpretation of Suspected Pediatric Acute Appendicitis: The Role of Pediatric Subspecialty Training.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Magnetic resonance diagnosis of pediatric acute appendicitis is highly accurate but may vary depending on reader training and subspecialty expertise. The study aims to compare the diagnostic performance of fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists and nonpediatric fellowship-trained emergency radiologists for non-contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) diagnosis of suspected pediatric acute appendicitis (AA). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Retrospective, single-center study including 122 patients who underwent non-contrast-enhanced MRI for clinical concern of AA, following equivocal or inconclusive ultrasound. Reference standard based on clinical follow-up and surgical notes. Two fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists and two nonpediatric fellowship-trained emergency radiologists independently reviewed the examinations using a standardized yes/no case report form. Paired comparisons used McNemar's test. Predictive values are reported descriptively with 95% confidence intervals, with between-groups differences assessed using case-level bootstrap resampling. Appendix visualization was analyzed descriptively only. RESULTS: The cohort included 122 patients (63 male [51.6%], 59 female [48.4%]; median age 11 years, IQR 7-13 years, range 4-18 years), of whom 31 (25.4%) had pathology-confirmed AA. Sensitivity for MRI diagnosis of AA was similar between groups (fellowship-trained pediatric 87.1% [71.1-94.9] vs nonpediatric fellowship-trained 90.3% [75.1-96.7]; P = 1.00), with higher specificity among pediatric radiologists (97.8% [92.3-99.4] vs 84.6% [75.8-90.6]; P = 0.002). Specificity was also higher among pediatric radiologists for direct signs (98.9% [94.0-99.8] vs 86.8% [78.4-92.3]; P = 0.001) and for combined direct and indirect signs (98.9% vs 92.3%; P = 0.03), as was accuracy for MRI diagnosis of AA (95.1% [89.7-97.7] vs 86.1% [78.8-91.1]; P = 0.03) and for direct signs (94.3% vs 86.1%; P = 0.03). Positive predictive value was higher among pediatric radiologists for the diagnosis of AA, direct signs, and combined direct and indirect signs, reaching 96.2% (81.1-99.3) vs 68.4% (52.5-80.9) for direct signs (P < 0.001). Negative predictive value did not differ in any category. Interpretation time was longer for pediatric radiologists, with a median paired difference of 23.5 seconds (P = 0.04). CONCLUSION: Fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists had higher specificity, positive predictive value, and accuracy than non-pediatric emergency radiologists for MRI diagnosis of suspected pediatric AA, with a small difference in interpretation time (median, 24 seconds). These findings, based on a limited number of readers, suggest differences in subspecialty expertise and aims and support further multicenter evaluation.

articles.title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Chest X-Ray Radiomic Model for Identifying PRISm in Non-COPD Individuals.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Chest X-ray (CXR) is low-cost and widely accessible but lacks effective tools for identifying preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm). This study aimed to develop and validate a CXR-based radiomics-clinical combined model for PRISm screening. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Paired CXR images and clinical variables from 9 hospitals were retrospectively collected between January 2017 and December 2023. Bilateral lung fields on CXR were segmented with a fully automated segmentation algorithm. PyRadiomics was adopted to extract radiomic features. Clinical, radiomic, and combined models were established. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis with DeLong's test for intermodel area under the curve (AUC) comparison. Global and local SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses were performed to interpret the model. RESULTS: A total of 1563 participants (mean age, 63.1 ± 12.0 years; 857 males; 422 PRISm cases) were included. The combined model achieved optimal performance, with AUCs of 0.761, 0.753, and 0.759 across the training, internal, and external validation cohorts. In the external validation cohort, the combined model (AUC = 0.759, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.658-0.854) significantly outperformed individual radiomic (AUC = 0.618, 95% CI: 0.505-0.732) and clinical models (AUC = 0.655, 95% CI: 0.549-0.760; all p < 0.001). SHAP analysis revealed sex as the top predictor in the combined model, followed by radiomic features, body mass index, age, and smoking status. Local SHAP visualizations illustrated variable feature contributions for individual PRISm and normal spirometry cases. CONCLUSIONS: The CXR-based combined model exhibits favorable stability and diagnostic performance for PRISm identification, supporting its utility as a primary-screening tool. The SHAP method enhanced the model's interpretability and clinical applicability.

articles.title: Informed Consent and Risk Presentations by Radiology Trainees for Core Liver Biopsies: Shortcomings and Opportunities for Improvement.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Informed consent is both a legal and ethical requirement and an interpersonal communication. The quality and completeness of consent discussions may influence patients' perceptions of risk, anxiety, confidence, and procedural experience. The goal of this study was to evaluate how trainees conduct informed consent to patients undergoing core liver biopsies. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Fifty consent conversations were recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed. The conversations were assessed for content, completeness, and presentation. Three levels of completeness (basic, intermediate, and advanced) were based on published standards. Inductive and deductive qualitative content analysis was used to find patterns in the coded data. Patients' anxiety, confidence, and pain perception were measured before the consent and after the procedure. The age, sex, post-graduate year, and race of the trainees were recorded to assess the effects of these factors. RESULTS: Twenty-seven of fifty consent conversations (54%) met the predefined criteria for basic consent completeness. Eight conversations (16%) met criteria for intermediate completeness, and one conversation (2%) met criteria for advanced completeness. The patients reported no change in their anxiety, pain, or confidence from before the consent to after the procedure. No effect could be attributed to trainees' characteristics. Consent conversations were insufficiently detailed for the evaluation of risk framing strategies or for conversation analysis. CONCLUSION: The informed consent conversation, as conducted by radiology trainees, is often incomplete and insubstantial. Trainees need guidance on the essential content of informed consent, how to frame risk, and how to engage patients in a two-way discussion.

articles.title: Age and sex differences in T1 relaxation times and volumetrics in segmented brain and upper cervical spine in healthy participants using MP2RAGE protocol at 3.0 T.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: To examine the influence of age and sex on T1 relaxation and volume in brain and upper cervical cord using MP2RAGE, which offers high contrast-to-noise ratio, uniform tissue contrast, and superior anatomical resolution alongside T1 mapping. This provides an accurate analysis of the magnitude of the effects of these covariates on the outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: 208 MP2RAGE scans from the Max Planck Institute Leipzig Mind-Brain-Body LEMON dataset were segmented and labeled using FreeSurfer and Spinal Cord Toolbox. The influences of age and sex on dependent variables were analyzed using linear regression and group difference were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. RESULTS: T1 values of cortical gray matter (GM), cerebral white matter (WM), thalamus, caudate, putamen, hippocampus, amygdala, and anterior corpus callosum (CC) varied significantly with age. Cortical GM and cervical C1 T1 showed statistical significance with sex, with latter lower in the females compared to males. T1 values of the posterior CC were significantly lower than the anterior portion. GM, WM, thalamus, caudate, putamen, hippocampus and anterior CC volumes were significantly affected by age. Spine cross-sectional area (CSA) showed statistically significant differences with sex but not age. CONCLUSIONS: T1, regional brain volumes, and spinal CSA vary according to anatomical location, age, and sex, reflecting physiological differences associated with aging and sex. These results can operate as a normative baseline to gauge the magnitude of effect of these covariates on future studies in health or disease.

articles.title: Atlas-assisted segment anything model for fetal brain MRI (FeTal-SAM).
articles.abstract: This paper presents FeTal-SAM, a novel adaptation of the Segment Anything Model (SAM) tailored for fetal brain MRI segmentation. Traditional deep learning methods often require large annotated datasets for a fixed set of labels, making them inflexible when clinical or research needs change. By integrating atlas-based prompts and foundation-model principles, FeTal-SAM addresses two key limitations in fetal brain MRI segmentation: (1) the need to retrain models for varying label definitions, and (2) the lack of insight into whether segmentations are driven by genuine image contrast or merely inferred by learned spatial priors. We leverage multi-atlas registration to generate spatially aligned label templates that serve as dense prompts, alongside a bounding-box prompt, for SAM's segmentation decoder. This strategy enables binary segmentation on a per-structure basis, which is subsequently fused to reconstruct the full 3D segmentation volumes. Evaluations on two datasets, the dHCP dataset and an in-house dataset demonstrate FeTal-SAM's robust performance across gestational ages. Notably, it achieves Dice scores comparable to state-of-the-art baselines which were trained for each dataset and label definition for well-contrasted structures like cortical plate and cerebellum, while maintaining the flexibility to segment anatomical structures that could be templated by compatible atlas image and label sample pairs. Although slightly lower accuracy is observed for subtle, low-contrast structures (e.g., hippocampus, amygdala), our results highlight FeTal-SAM's potential as a flexible atlas-conditioned segmentation framework without requiring a separately trained model for each supported parcellation. This method thus constitutes a promising step toward clinically adaptable fetal brain MRI analysis tools.

articles.title: Altered language network microstructure links with impaired language function and development in very preterm/very low birth weight born adults.
articles.abstract: Premature birth is associated with impaired language function. In premature-born children, language function has been linked with microstructural alterations of the language network.Whether these brain-language associations persist into adulthood remains unclear. We investigated the microstructural properties of major dorsal and ventral language pathways in very preterm/very low birth weight (VPT/VLBW) adults and their associations with language performance in adulthood and childhood. Sixty-three VPT/VLBW and eighty full-term-born adults (mean age 26.8 years) underwent diffusion-weighted imaging and language assessment. The arcuate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus were reconstructed using probabilistic tractography from which fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) measures were extracted. Adult language function was assessed via the Regensburg word fluency test, rapid automatized naming and verbal IQ; childhood language was assessed at the mean age of 8 using the Kaufman Assessment Battery for children. We observed altered language network microstructure in VPT/VLBW participants, illustrated by lower FA and higher MD in the SLF and UF. These microstructural alterations were associated with language function in adulthood, but also with language development in childhood. We found that the association between tract microstructure and language abilities differed between groups. Our results demonstrate altered language network microstructure in premature born adults, which links with impaired language function and development. These findings extend previous work by comprehensively characterizing the adult dorsal and ventral language network and relating its microstructural properties to language function across development. The selective follow-up sample may limit generalizability to the broader VPT/VLBW population.

articles.title: Planned versus accumulated dose in radiotherapy of oropharyngeal carcinoma - Do recurrences occur in unintended cold spots?
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Locoregional recurrence (LRR) in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) patients treated with radiotherapy (RT) most often occurs within the high-dose target volume. Anatomical changes during RT may potentially lead to unintended target underdosage, which could contribute to the risk of treatment failure. This study aimed to quantify differences between planned and accumulated dose in the regions of later LRR. METHODS: Patients treated with curatively intended RT for OPSCC between 2009 and 2017 at Rigshospitalet with biopsy-proven LRR were identified. Recurrence volumes were delineated on follow up imaging and mapped to the planning CT. The point of origin (PO) of each recurrence was determined using the nidus method. Dose accumulation was performed using synthetic CTs based on daily cone beam CT, followed by recalculation and summation of daily dose distributions. Planned and accumulated doses at the PO were compared. Additional analyses evaluated effect of deformable registration methods. RESULTS: Forty patients with 54 recurrence volumes were included. The accumulated dose was higher than the planned dose in 57% of recurrences. The mean difference between accumulated and planned dose at the PO was - 0.04 Gy (SD: 0.81; 95% CI: -0.26 to 0.18 Gy; p = 0.72). Neither PO localization nor the dose accumulation process was sensitive to the use of an alternative deformation software CONCLUSIONS: Within the evaluated setting, no evidence was found that regions of later LRR were systematically underdosed. Dose differences were small and within clinically acceptable limits. This suggests that anatomical changes during RT were unlikely to cause clinically relevant compromised target dose coverage.

articles.title: Harmonizing spatially fractionated radiation therapy: consensus and roadmap from an ESTRO workshop.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Spatially fractionated radiation therapy (SFRT) intentionally delivers nonuniform dose distributions characterized by alternating high-dose peaks and low-dose valleys, with therapeutic potential for complex, inoperable bulky tumors. Although clinical adoption is expanding, clinical implementation and practices remain heterogeneous across institutions. This consensus aims to identify system-level barriers to harmonized clinical implementation of SFRT and formulate consensus-based recommendations to enable reproducible multi-institutional integration. METHODS: The 2025 ESTRO Physics Workshop convened multidisciplinary international experts to evaluate current implementation practices and develop harmonization priorities through structured consensus discussions. Twenty-eight delegates participated, representing centers across Europe, the United States, China, and Australia. Core domains included dose recording and reporting specifications, commissioning and quality assurance (QA), motion management, registry infrastructure, and governance. RESULTS: Five principal domains were identified as barriers to harmonized implementation: (1) inconsistent dose recording and reporting conventions; (2) variability in commissioning and QA practices for heterogeneous small-field dose distributions; (3) uncertainty in motion management and geometric robustness evaluation in the presence of anatomical changes; (4) fragmented data infrastructure limiting multi-institutional outcome analysis; and (5) limited coordinated governance and standardization infrastructure. Consensus recommendations and a phased roadmap with measurable milestones were formulated to address these domains. CONCLUSION: Harmonization of clinical implementation is essential to ensure reproducibility, support prospective multi-institutional trials, and safeguard consistent patient care across institutions. Coordinated international collaboration will be critical to establish standardized definitions, QA benchmarks, registry infrastructure, and governance frameworks for safe and effective clinical integration.

articles.title: Cognitive outcomes of low-dose whole-brain radiation therapy in mild Alzheimer's disease: A multicenter, randomized, sham-controlled phase II clinical trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) has shown potential in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD) models, but controlled clinical evidence is limited. We evaluated two whole-brain LDRT regimens in mild AD. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this multicenter, participant-blinded, three-arm phase II trial, amyloid-positive participants were randomized 1:1:1 to sham irradiation, 0.04 Gy per fraction (0.24 Gy total), or 0.5 Gy per fraction (3 Gy total), delivered twice weekly for 3 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-cog) score from baseline to 6 months. Twelve-month analyses were exploratory. Longitudinal outcomes were estimated using mixed-effects models. RESULTS: Forty-one participants were randomized; 36 were included in the modified intention-to-treat population and 30 completed 12-month follow-up. At 6 months, adjusted between-group differences in ADAS-cog change versus sham were -2.08 points (95% CI, -7.06 to 2.89; p = 0.401) for 0.24 Gy and -2.92 points (95% CI, -6.72 to 0.89; p = 0.129) for 3 Gy. At 12 months, the corresponding exploratory differences were -3.02 points (95% CI, -10.00 to 3.96; p = 0.386) and -5.36 points (95% CI, -10.58 to -0.14; nominal p = 0.044). No treatment-related adverse events or radiologic safety concerns were identified. CONCLUSIONS: The prespecified 6-month primary endpoint was not met. Exploratory 12-month and secondary analyses showed differences in selected cognitive outcomes, although the findings varied across doses and outcomes. These findings did not establish efficacy or a dose-response relationship and warrant confirmation in a larger trial with longer follow-up.

articles.title: DAG-informed analysis of muscle characteristics and overall survival in patients receiving radical treatment for bladder cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reduced skeletal muscle (SM) quantity and quality may influence outcomes in bladder cancer, but most studies are associative and vulnerable to confounding and inconsistent covariate adjustment. We applied a directed acyclic graph (DAG)-informed framework to evaluate associations between computed tomography-derived SM characteristics and overall survival (OS) in patients receiving curative-intent radiotherapy-based bladder preservation or radical cystectomy. METHODS: This retrospective two-centre cohort study included patients treated between 2014 and 2024. Computed tomography imaging closest to definitive local therapy was analysed using an automated segmentation pipeline to quantify SM quantity, expressed as skeletal muscle index (SMI), and quality, expressed as intramuscular adipose tissue ratio (IMATR). A DAG was used to prespecify the adjustment strategy, and Cox models were fitted separately within radiotherapy and surgical cohorts. RESULTS: The final cohorts comprised 353 radiotherapy-treated and 117 surgically treated patients. In the radiotherapy cohort, higher SMI was associated with improved OS (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.66-0.94, p = 0.007), while higher IMATR was associated with worse OS (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.04-1.48, p = 0.014). In the smaller surgical cohort, point estimates were directionally discordant with the radiotherapy findings and imprecise: SMI HR 1.35 (95% CI 0.99-1.85, p = 0.057) and IMATR HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.62-1.21, p = 0.39). CONCLUSIONS: In this DAG-informed analysis, higher SMI and lower IMATR were associated with improved OS in radiotherapy-treated patients. Surgical estimates were imprecise and should be considered exploratory. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support further evaluation of CT-derived muscle characteristics as prognostic markers within radiotherapy-treated populations but cannot yet establish a differential benefit for radiotherapy vs cystectomy.

articles.title: Quantitative Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer Imaging With Golden-Angle Radial k-Space Sampling and Locally Low-Rank Reconstruction.
articles.abstract: Chemical exchange saturation transfer magnetic resonance fingerprinting (CEST-MRF) is a promising quantitative molecular imaging technique. To reduce scan time, current CEST-MRF implementations typically use echo-planar imaging (EPI) readouts, which are prone to geometric distortion and signal dropout. In this study, we developed a motion-robust, geometrically accurate CEST-MRF method using radial k-space sampling, locally low-rank reconstruction, and neural network-based quantification. The acquisition schedule was optimized using deep learning, and its accuracy was validated in numerical simulations with digital phantoms. The number of spokes per measurement was determined through simulations and in vivo ablation studies in healthy volunteers. Five healthy subjects underwent repeated scans, and regions of interest were defined for analysis. Tissue maps generated with the proposed method were compared with values obtained from nonlinear least-squares (NLS) fitting of multisaturation-power z-spectra. Motion sensitivity and test-retest reproducibility were evaluated using the coefficient of variation (CV) and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Clinical feasibility was demonstrated in a subject with a history of remote middle cerebral artery infarction. The results show that 3D quantitative CEST maps can be acquired in 11 min using 34 spokes per measurement. Numerical simulations yielded mean errors below 14% for all tissue parameters, while in vivo parameter estimates agreed well with both NLS-derived values and prior brain CEST-MRF studies. The mean ICC across all tissue maps was 0.92 in white matter and 0.87 in gray matter, with mean intersubject CVs of 5.4% and 3.4%, respectively. The mean error between motion and no-motion conditions was 8.6%. In the pathology case, changes in CEST-MRF tissue parameters were consistent with clinically diagnosed cystic gliosis. This approach enables accurate and reproducible 3D quantitative CEST imaging of the brain within clinically feasible scan times.

articles.title: Automated carotid artery atherosclerotic inflammation segmentation in PET using MSR-Net.
articles.abstract: AbstractObjective. To develop an automated method for segmentation and uptake quantification ofcarotid atherosclerotic inflammation on 64Cu-CANF-comb PET while accounting forpartial-volume and tissue-fraction effects.Approach. Synthetic carotid PET images with known fractional-volume ground truth weregenerated by combining MR-derived high-resolution activity maps with GATE MonteCarlo simulation incorporating major PET physical processes and matched to theBiograph mMR acquisition and reconstruction. A two-stage network first localized thecarotid vessel wall from T1-weighted MR and then estimated voxel-wise inflammationfraction from masked PET. Both stages used a multiscale residual (MSR) convolutionalbackbone. Performance was compared with U-Net, Transformer U-Net, DUCK-Net, anditerative Yang partial-volume correction.Main results. In a two-alternative forced-choice study, five nuclear-medicine physiciansidentified real images with 54% accuracy (54/100; Wilson 95% CI 0.44-0.63; exactbinomial p = 0.48). On 184 simulated test slices from five held-out patients, the proposedmethod achieved a weighted DSC of 0.79, compared with 0.73 for U-Net, 0.69 forTransformer U-Net, and 0.75 for DUCK-Net, with corresponding HD values of 1.85, 2.29,2.32, and 2.23 voxels. Patient-cluster bootstrap comparisons favored the proposed methodfor DSC and HD against all three baselines (Holm-corrected p ≤ 0.031). Overall ENRMSEwas 0.24 versus 0.59, 0.68, and 0.59 for the three DL baselines and 0.57 for iterative Yang.In seven patients, corrected SUV showed a positive association with MR-derivedlipid-rich/necrotic core with hemorrhage.Significance. The proposed framework improved carotid PET segmentation and uptakequantification under simulated conditions. The patient analysis is preliminary and requiresexternal validation with biological reference standards before clinical deployment.

articles.title: An experimentally calibrated nanodosimetry-based framework for predicting LET-dependent relative biological effectiveness in proton boron capture therapy.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Proton boron capture therapy (PBCT) studies focus on physical dose enhancement or biological observations, while quantitative prediction of biological effectiveness remains limited. This study aimed to establish a framework combining Monte Carlo (MC) simulation, nanodosimetry, and radiobiological experiments to evaluate the relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of PBCT. APPROACH: Geant4-based MC simulations and a pre-calculated nanodosimetric database were used to determine mixed-field nanodosimetric parameters, including M1, M2, and F2. Clonogenic survival experiments were performed using a clinical 70 MeV proton beam and a 6 MV photon beam. U-87 MG cells were irradiated with photons, protons, and PBCT at 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 Gy using boronophenylalanine (BPA, 21.0 ppm 11B). Survival data were fitted with the linear-quadratic model, and the resulting α and β values were used to optimize the Logistic Nanodosimetry Model (LNDM) for depth-dependent RBE prediction. MAIN RESULTS: The LNDM, combined with MC-derived nanodosimetric parameters and experimental survival data, reproduced the measured radiobiological response with differences in α and β below 0.5% at the experimental cell position, corresponding to a water-equivalent depth (WED) of 3.9 cm and located on the rising edge of the Bragg peak. PBCT consistently exhibited higher α and RBE values than proton irradiation across the investigated LET range. At 3.9 cm, PBCT increased RBE by 8.7% compared with protons. For the 70 MeV beam, PBCT yielded α = 0.116 Gy⁻¹, β = 0.023 Gy⁻², and RBE = 1.25, compared with α = 0.076 Gy⁻¹, β = 0.023 Gy⁻², and RBE = 1.15 for proton therapy. SIGNIFICANCE: An experimentally calibrated framework integrating MC simulation, nanodosimetry, radiobiological experiments, and the LNDM was established for LET-dependent PBCT RBE prediction based on biological calibration data. PBCT showed consistently higher RBE than proton therapy, with a greater advantage at higher LET, supporting future biological optimization of PBCT.

articles.title: Time-aware frame-aligned diffusion-inspired model for late dynamic PET frame prediction from early [11C] raclopride.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To reduce the burden of dynamic PET acquisition while preserving quantitative analysis, we propose a time-aware frame-aligned diffusion-inspired residual denoising framework for predicting late dynamic PET frames from a short early acquisition window (10 min in this study) of [¹¹C] raclopride. APPROACH: Irregular native dynamic frames were converted to a uniform 1-min indexing grid using overlap-weighted rebinning. The first 10 min were used as the early input and to derive the spatial and intensity preprocessing parameters. For each requested late time, a shared time-aware 3D U-Net predicted an anchor-relative residual with respect to the last available early frame. A training-only DDPM-inspired Gaussian perturbation and noise-prediction branch shared the prediction backbone and regularized residual learning, while temporal-consistency loss constrained predicted frame-to-frame changes. All learning-based methods used identical subject-wise five-fold cross-validation within the development cohort, followed by evaluation on a fixed internal test set; the external cohort was held out from model selection. MAIN RESULTS: The proposed approach achieved higher PSNR and SSIM and lower MAE than the comparison methods, while providing closer agreement with reference TACs and SRTM-derived parameter estimates across the limbic, associative, and sensorimotor striata. SIGNIFICANCE: The proposed framework provides deterministic time-resolved late-frame estimates from early dynamic PET while using a DDPM-inspired noise-prediction objective only as an auxiliary training regularizer rather than as an iterative diffusion inference process. This design may support shortened dynamic PET protocols while retaining TAC and kinetic-parameter fidelity.

articles.title: Enhancements and reference internal dosimetry data for the MOBY whole-body computational phantom of the laboratory mouse.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Computational phantoms play a crucial role in preclinical studies, particularly for internal dosimetry applications. While the mouse whole-body (MOBY) phantom has been widely used in Monte Carlo radiation transport simulations, several anatomical limitations restrict its dosimetric accuracy. This study introduces enhanced tetrahedral mesh-based MOBY phantoms, in male and female version, featuring refined skeletal structures, improved anatomical representation, and an extended and standardized blood distribution model to support small animal dosimetry. METHODS: The MOBY polygon mesh representation served as the foundation for phantom development. Using the 3D modeling software, Blender, organ and skeletal structures were refined to eliminate mesh intersections while preserving anatomical integrity. The skeleton was segmented into cortical, spongiosa and medullary cavity regions, and a spinal cord was incorporated into the vertebral foramina. The male model was finalized by adding a prostate and subsequently modified to create the female counterpart by replacing male-specific structures with the uterus and ovaries. Additional anatomical refinements included lymph nodes, Peyer's patches, bronchial wall and primary blood vessels, with organ-specific blood volumes calculated for estimating bulk tissue densities. Each phantom was rigidly scaled to yield six phantoms of different total body mass for each sex. RESULTS: A total of twelve anatomically enhanced MOBY phantoms were developed in tetrahedral format. Monte Carlo radiation transport simulations were performed and SAFs and S-values for different radionuclides were computed, establishing a robust dataset for preclinical radiation dosimetry for inclusion in the MIRDcalc software code. CONCLUSIONS: The refined MOBY phantoms provide a critical advancement in preclinical dosimetry by incorporating sex-specific anatomical details, an improved skeletal model, and enhanced organ-level dose assessments. These phantoms will facilitate dose-response radiopharmaceutical research and support the integration of murine dosimetry models into human dose estimation frameworks.

articles.title: Influence of x-ray beam quality on retrospective bone dose estimation in a murine model: experimental investigation of EPR signal kinetics and computational modeling.
articles.abstract: In the context of radiological accidents, retrospective dosimetry methods such as electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy and Monte Carlo simulation are used for dose reconstruction. EPR analysis of bone biopsies allows experimental assessment of absorbed dose. However, several factors may affect EPR dose estimation. The time delay between irradiation and sampling can lead to underestimation of absorbed dose to bone, and the influence of beam quality needs investigation.
