Therefore, this study aims to evaluate the influence of X-ray beam quality on bone EPR signal kinetics and the absorbed dose distribution in bone.Approach: A murine model of localized hind limb irradiation was developed using three beam qualities (50 kVp, 220 kVp, 10 MV). EPR measurements were performed to characterize radio-induced free radical kinetics in bone collected at different time points, from irradiation day to six months post-irradiation. A computational model of the irradiation setup was implemented in GEANT4 to study the dose distribution and complement the experimental observations.Main results: High-energy X-rays (10 MV) led to a rapid decrease in EPR signal, with 75% signal loss after 21 days and no detectable signal under our conditions after 42 days. For low-energy X-rays, the signal decreased more rapidly at 220 kVp than at 50 kVp, with signal loss of 51% and 31% respectively at 21 days, and a residual EPR signal remains at later time points (70-80% signal loss at six months). Monte Carlo simulations highlighted heterogeneous dose deposition between tissues with low-energy X-rays, as well as significant beam attenuation within mouse tibia for 50 kVp X-rays, leading to inhomogeneous dose deposition in bone.Significance: Using a preclinical model, we have demonstrated that X-ray beam quality and time affect bone dose estimation. These findings improve our understanding of how radiation quality and bone physiology affect outcomes over time after irradiation.

articles.title: Electron specific absorbed fractions for the ICRP family of mesh-type reference computational phantoms.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To provide electron specific absorbed fractions (SAFs) using the mesh-type reference computational phantoms (MRCPs) developed by the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP). APPROACH: The ICRP family of MRCPs from Publications 145 and 156 supersedes the voxel-type reference computational phantoms (VRCPs) used in ICRP Publications 133 and 155. Unlike the VRCPs, the MRCPs can explicitly define micrometer-scale radiosensitive target tissues and include intra-organ blood content. Electron SAFs were computed for all 12 MRCPs using the PHITS Monte Carlo code, covering 86 source regions and 62 target regions. Total electron SAFs were obtained using a component-based method that separates collisional and radiative contributions, with the latter derived from our companion photon SAF datasets. Results for the adult male MRCP were independently verified against Geant4 calculations. MAIN RESULTS: The MRCP-based electron SAF datasets showed agreement with ICRP Publications 133 and 155 for self-absorption geometries across the full energy range. For crossfire geometries, differences were observed and are likely attributable to several factors, including revised organ geometries, the representation of micrometer-scale target tissue layers, the use of different photon datasets for the radiative SAFs, and differing low-energy extrapolation methods. Age-dependent trends were observed, with younger reference individuals often yielding higher SAF values. General agreement was observed between PHITS and Geant4 across the full energy range and source-target combinations considered. SIGNIFICANCE: To the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to provide complete electron SAF datasets spanning all ICRP MRCPs with expanded source-target combinations.

articles.title: Correction of arterial input-function saturation for extraction fraction estimation in retinal fluorescein videoangiography.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Quantitative retinal fluorescein videoangiography (FVA) can estimate extraction fraction (E), but the 8-bit intensity resolution of clinical systems creates a dynamic-range tradeoff: preserving arterial input function (AIF) linearity can restrict tissue signal, particularly for pixel-level analysis. We developed a single-bolus correction method to broaden the usable acquisition range while maintaining E estimation accuracy. APPROACH: The method combined truncated-mean reconstruction when sufficient unsaturated arterial pixels remained with gamma-variate interpolation when saturation dominated the first-pass peak. Development simulations used four human-derived AIF templates, empirically characterized signal-dependent noise, and 20 paired realizations evaluated over arterial scaling factors f = 0.1-2.25. Tissue curves were generated using a distributed-transit-time AATH model and fitted using a plug-flow AATH model. The locked correction threshold was then evaluated by artificially clipping raw arterial-pixel time curves from 10 originally undersaturated FVAs without adding synthetic noise. Performance was compared with the clipped arterial mean, PCHIP, and gamma-variate interpolation alone. MAIN RESULTS: The combined method completed all 60 patient-by-clipping analyses and produced lower first-pass peak, normalized mean squared error, and area-under-the-curve errors than the comparator methods under moderate-to-strong clipping. In kinetic simulations, mean absolute relative ROI E error with the uncorrected AIF increased from 17 ± 9% at f = 1.25 to 60 ± 20% at f = 2.25, whereas corrected-AIF error remained approximately 10-20%. Single-pixel E error decreased as signal approached the detector ceiling, reached 17 ± 11% at f = 1.75, and remained statistically similar across f = 0.8-2.0. No single-pixel fits failed at f ≥ 1.0. SIGNIFICANCE: The correction framework converts modest AIF saturation from a restrictive acquisition limit into a manageable analytical condition. This broader operating range is valuable for 8-bit FVA, supporting acquisition near the detector ceiling to improve tissue signal and enable high-resolution E mapping without dual-bolus acquisition.

articles.title: Untangling the causes of elongation artifacts in dual flat-panel PET: limited angular sampling versus parallax error.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Dual flat-panel PET systems provide easy patient access and high sensitivity when the panels are close together. Their images are however susceptible to elongation artifacts due to incomplete angular sampling and parallax error. These effects are reduced by respectively including depth-of-interaction (DOI) and time-of-flight (TOF) information. To guide system design, a framework is needed that predicts which effect dominates for a given object size and field-of-view (FOV) location. This study investigates the impact of TOF and DOI on elongation artifacts for a variety of phantoms in a dual flat-panel system, benchmarked against a cylindrical reference. APPROACH: A large dual flat-panel system and cylindrical system with the same axial FOV were simulated. The TOF and DOI resolution were varied independently and iterative MLEM reconstruction was performed. Data were generated for point sources and spheres spanning 1-50 mm radius at multiple FOV positions. Point-source blur was quantified with full width at half maximum measurements, and sphere elongation using an activity-spillover metric. Findings were validated using the more clinically relevant NEMA IQ and XCAT phantoms with embedded lesions. MAIN RESULTS: DOI uncertainty resulted in elongations independently of object size. In the cylindrical system, these only occurred at radial offsets, but in the dual flat-panel system, parallax-blur was also present at the center of the FOV. Elongations due to limited angular coverage in the flat-panel system grew with object size and dominated for features over 1-2 cm. The extent of these elongations increased towards the FOV edges and was substantially reduced by including TOF information. With adequate TOF and DOI performance, the flat-panel system matched cylindrical image quality. SIGNIFICANCE: The framework predicts the dominant artifact mechanism as a function of object size, position, and system geometry. The insights guide detector and system design for dual flat-panel PET and corresponding artifact correction methods.

articles.title: Ultrasound in fetal growth restriction.
articles.abstract: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is associated with increased perinatal morbidity and mortality. Its recognition requires differentiation from a constitutionally small-for-gestational-age (SGA) fetus. Based on the current AWMF S2k guideline, this CME review summarizes the ultrasound assessment and clinical management of suspected FGR. Accurate first-trimester dating, standardized fetal biometry, assessment of amniotic fluid volume, and detailed anatomical evaluation form the basis of diagnosis. Consensus-based criteria distinguish early FGR before 32 + 0 weeks' gestation from late FGR at or beyond 32 + 0 weeks' gestation. Multivessel Doppler assessment of the umbilical artery, middle cerebral artery, cerebroplacental ratio, and ductus venosus provides complementary information on placental resistance, fetal redistribution, and cardiovascular decompensation. Cardiotocography, including computerized analysis of short-term variation in early FGR, is used as part of multimodal surveillance and should not be interpreted in isolation. The review discusses appropriate monitoring intervals, indications for inpatient care, antenatal corticosteroids and fetal neuroprotection when preterm birth is anticipated, as well as gestational-age- and finding-dependent timing and mode of delivery. A practical clinical case illustrates the diagnostic pathway from abnormal fetal biometry to delivery planning.

articles.title: Segment anything model (SAM)-driven prompt-guided interactive delineation of gross tumor volume for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Segment Anything Model (SAM), a prompt-guided foundation model, exhibits substantial potential for medical image segmentation by incorporating prior knowledge through user-defined prompts. However, the application of SAM in radiotherapy target delineation remains limited. PURPOSE: This study proposes a feasible prompt-guided interactive delineation workflow driven by an optimized SAM. METHODS: A total of 100 rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy cases were collected (60 for training and 40 for testing). This study utilized bounding-box prompts to guide SAM for GTV segmentation. Physicians manually draw box prompts on certain slices, while box prompts for the remaining slices are automatically generated using an interpolation strategy. Four fine-tuning strategies for SAM training were evaluated, and the impact of prompt numbers and placements was assessed as well. The performance of the finalized workflow with optimized SAM was compared with five state-of-the-art (SOTA) models, and its robustness to prompt variations in middle-slice selection and box-prompt margins was analyzed. RESULTS: Compared to other fine-tuning methods, freezing the image encoder obtained the most stable performance. Prompts on only 3 slices achieved accuracy comparable to prompts on all slices. The placement of the middle-slice prompt exhibited negligible impact (p > 0.05). The finalized SAM-driven workflow outperformed end-to-end baseline models both visually and quantitatively (3D DSC: 0.92 vs 0.80; 3D HD95: 2.73 vs 12.70; IoU: 0.86 vs 0.67; Sensitivity: 91.20% vs 85.98%; Precision: 93.65% vs 79.23%), while maintaining stable performance across certain prompt variations. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed SAM-driven interactive workflow with as few as 3 box prompts achieves favorable accuracy of GTV segmentation for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.

articles.title: Evaluation of quantitative accuracy in 4D DCE-bCT: Insights from a perfusion phantom study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Four-dimensional dynamic contrast-enhanced breast CT (4D DCE-bCT) provides submillimeter spatial resolution and temporal sampling within seconds, offering potential for improved perfusion assessment in breast cancer. Its quantitative accuracy, however, must be validated. PURPOSE: To evaluate the accuracy of dynamic iodine concentration quantification in 4D DCE-bCT using a perfusion phantom with in-line optical spectroscopy and ultraviolet-visible (UV/VIS) spectrophotometry as reference standards. METHODS: A dynamic flow phantom with a 3 mm internal diameter was used to approximate tumor-feeding vessels. Potassium iodide (KI) contrast was introduced using block-pulse injections at 1, 3, and 5 mg I/mL and a gradual inflow-outflow protocol to reproduce bolus passage. In-line optical spectroscopy and UV/VIS spectrophotometry provided reference measurements. Dynamic bCT acquisitions were performed using a previously developed sparse-view protocol. A static pre-contrast scan was reconstructed with the iterative maximum-likelihood polychromatic algorithm for CT (IMPACT), and post-contrast dynamic scans were reconstructed using the prior image constrained compressed sensing (PICCS) algorithm. Acquisitions were performed at 65 kV with 0.25 mm Cu filtration, 80 mA for the pre-contrast scan (300 projections over 10 s) and 32 mA for the post-contrast scans (444 projections per 100 s), using a 5 ms pulse width. Projection data were corrected for scatter and motion before reconstruction, and the static prior was then subtracted from post-contrast volumes. Object-size effects were evaluated using the 3 mm tube and 5, 10, 15, and 20 mm hollow spheres filled with non-flowing iodine at 1, 3, and 5 mg I/mL. The tube interior was segmented using thresholding and morphological cleanup, while spherical phantoms were segmented by identifying the sphere center and extracting all enclosed voxels. Voxel values were converted to iodine concentration using a pre-determined calibration curve, and agreement with reference standards was evaluated using peak concentrations and time-concentration profiles, with errors reported as absolute and relative differences. RESULTS: In dynamic block-pulse experiments, peak iodine concentrations measured by 4D DCE-bCT were systematically underestimated relative to ground truth, with relative errors of approximately 12% to 39%. In gradual inflow-outflow experiments, the peak iodine concentration derived from 4D DCE-bCT was 5.24 ± 0.61 mg I/mL, whereas optical ground truth measured 5.17 mg I/mL. Static experiments demonstrated an average underestimation of 0.23 ± 0.14 mg I/mL across target sizes and concentrations and no relationship between iodine estimation and target size. CONCLUSION: 4D DCE-bCT enabled acquisition of time-varying iodine concentration profiles in a 3 mm tube phantom. Gradual changes were captured more accurately compared to rapid changes, consistent with temporal averaging. These results demonstrate the feasibility of dynamic iodine imaging with 4D DCE-bCT while highlighting current limitations and motivating further evaluation in anatomically realistic phantoms and pilot clinical studies.

articles.title: Anatomical noise and visual realism assessment in simulated mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis images from data-driven breast phantoms.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Virtual imaging trials in medicine (VITMs) rely on in silico platforms that simulate tests on volunteers. In VITMs, a simulation software program replicates the imaging apparatus, and the patient is replaced by a digital phantom. Recent innovations in the field of x-ray breast imaging supported a widespread development of VITM platforms and the need for appropriate evaluations and validations. In this context, digital patients are usually created via mathematical models based on a priori anatomical assumptions, that permit the reproduction of a large population variability with arbitrarily fine spatial resolutions. On the other hand, data-driven digital phantoms-derived from 3D images of the breast-feature realistic shape and glandular tissue distribution; however, they are limited by the scarce availability of 3D breast images with relatively high image quality and by the spatial resolution of the used clinical data. These are largely adopted in dosimetry evaluations, but no single generally adopted criterion for realism evaluations-which depend on the intended clinical task-in simulated images exists. PURPOSE: This work aims to evaluate the realism of digital mammography (DM) and digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) images generated for VITMs by adopting data-driven digital breast phantoms via objective parameters and subjective analysis. METHODS: DM and DBT images were simulated via an open-source simulation platform. The cohort of data-driven digital breast phantoms included 126 cases from an open access database. The subjective analysis was conducted via a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) test and a Visual Grading Analysis (VGA) involving four radiologists. In the 2AFC test, radiologists were asked to recognize regions of interest (ROIs) extracted from simulated images, by comparison with a second set from clinical images. VGA evaluated image realisms based on a scoring scale. The objective analysis was conducted by evaluating the β parameter in images, this characterizing the magnitude of the anatomical noise. RESULTS: The β parameter was 2.71 ± 0.40 in DM and 3.09 ± 0.28 in DBT. From the analysis of the noise spectra of DM images, the presence of artifacts caused by the phantom voxelization was evident and prominent for thinner breasts. Radiologists distinguished ROIs from the simulated dataset from those from a clinical dataset in the vast majority of cases. Low pass filters on simulated images had little influence on DBT images; however, the sensitivity in detecting simulated images was no lower than 83%. VGA average scoring acknowledged some degree of image realism, outlining the presence of artifacts or unrealistic image regions. CONCLUSIONS: Objective evaluation reported that the β parameter evaluated for DM and DBT images simulated by adopting data-driven digital breast phantoms was in line with that from clinical images. A 2AFC test demonstrated that radiologists distinguish between simulated and real images. The subjective analysis also permitted the identification of the main features characterizing simulated images that include voxelization artifacts, the absence of fine structures and of a realistic adipose pattern in simulated images. However, realism should be verified with regard to a specific question of interest under investigation in a VITM.

articles.title: Self-supervised multi-contrast MRI reconstruction via mask-guided frequency-domain fusion.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Multi-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MC-MRI) enables detailed tissue characterization by acquiring multiple contrast-weighted images from the same anatomical region. Redundancy across contrasts can improve reconstruction from under-sampled data. However, conventional deep learning approaches rely on fully-sampled, contrast-aligned datasets, which require long acquisition times. Extended scanning durations not only increase patient burden but may also introduce physiological risks, limiting the practical adoption of accelerated MC-MRI in clinical settings. PURPOSE: This study introduces Self-MF, a self-supervised MC-MRI reconstruction framework that leverages contrast redundancy without requiring fully sampled target-contrast labels. The framework aims to provide a high-fidelity, scalable solution for reconstructing under-sampled multi-contrast images while preserving anatomical details and contrast fidelity. METHODS: Self-MF implements a contrast-aware self-supervised learning strategy that randomly partitions the acquired target k-space into input and held-out subsets, allowing the model to learn joint anatomical priors from under-sampled data without fully sampled target-contrast labels. A mask-guided frequency-domain conditioning module constructs reference-conditioned auxiliary frequency channels from auxiliary contrasts and acquired target measurements, enhancing the recovery of fine structural features during score-based reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on public datasets (IXI, fastMRI) and a clinical multi-coil dataset (SIAT), spanning multiple acceleration factors and undersampling patterns to assess robustness and generalizability. RESULTS: Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that Self-MF outperforms existing representative reconstruction methods across different contrasts, datasets, and acceleration factors. On the SIAT multi-contrast dataset, Self-MF achieved PSNR/SSIM values of 35.16/0.8870, 33.46/0.9054, and 35.31/0.9187 for T1WI, T2WI, and PDWI reconstruction under 2D random undersampling at R = 4, respectively. On the fastMRI brain dataset, Self-MF achieved 41.15 dB/0.9637 and 35.02 dB/0.8814 for T2WI reconstruction under R = 4 and R = 8, respectively, consistently outperforming the compared classical, learning-based, and diffusion-based baselines. CONCLUSIONS: Self-MF provides an effective, self-supervised solution for high-fidelity MC-MRI reconstruction without fully sampled target-contrast labels. By combining contrast-aware self-supervision, frequency-domain conditioning, and diffusion-based reconstruction, the framework achieves superior image quality and robust anatomical preservation, representing a significant advancement for multi-contrast MRI in both research and clinical practice.

articles.title: CT Perfusion in the differential diagnosis of glioblastomas and primary central nervous system lymphomas.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare perfusion parameters of glioblastomas and primary central nervous system lymphomas (PCNSL) using CT perfusion (CTP) and to assess the diagnostic performance of this technique for their preoperative differential diagnosis. METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included CTP data from 122 patients (57 with PCNSL and 65 with glioblastoma) examined at our hospital between 2006 and 2026. All diagnoses were histologically verified; no patient received chemotherapy, corticosteroids or radiotherapy prior to CTP. Imaging was performed on a 64-slice Optima 660 scanner (GE Medical Systems) using a prolonged perfusion protocol. Absolute (CBF, CBV, MTT, PS) and normalized (nCBF, nCBV, nMTT, nPS) perfusion parameters were obtained. The Mann-Whitney U test, Spearman correlation and ROC analysis were applied for statistical comparison. RESULTS: Glioblastomas demonstrated significantly higher CBF and CBV and lower MTT and PS values than PCNSL; the same pattern was observed for the normalized parameters. PS (AUC = 0.93), nPS (AUC = 0.90), nCBF (AUC = 0.91), nCBV (AUC = 0.90), CBF (AUC = 0.88) and CBV (AUC = 0.88) showed the highest diagnostic performance, whereas MTT and nMTT were less informative (AUC = 0.69-0.72). CONCLUSION: CTP is a highly informative non-invasive quantitative imaging tool for the preoperative differentiation of glioblastomas and PCNSL. The inclusion of normalized perfusion parameters improves reproducibility and supports use in routine clinical practice and multicenter studies. CTP can be recommended whenever conventional CT and MRI fail to reliably distinguish these tumors.

articles.title: Clinical evaluation of deep learning-based acquisition and reconstruction techniques for accelerated 2D shoulder magnetic resonance imaging acceleration at 3 T.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: GE has recently developed Sonic DL MRI acceleration technology. We wished to (1) quantify scanner time reduction compared to the AIR Recon DL already in clinical use at our institution and (2) preliminarily evaluate any change in diagnostic findings between these methods. METHODS: A total of 30 outpatients undergoing routine shoulder MRI for shoulder pain were recruited. Each underwent routine AIR Recon DL and Sonic DL exams containing the same sequences. Three subspecialized musculoskeletal radiologists assessed image quality, graded pathology, and reported diagnostic confidence in a blinded fashion. Differences in image quality and confidence were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. RESULTS: Sonic DL reduced nominal acquisition time 38.7% compared to AIR Recon DL (6 min 15 s versus 10 min 12 s). Artifact was considered slightly worse on the routine examination (3.20 versus 3.37, P = 0.039); there was no significant difference in image quality, sharpness, or signal-to-noise ratio between routine and Sonic DL accelerated exams (P 0.171-0.861). Inter-reader agreement was broadly similar between routine-routine and routine-Sonic DL comparisons (median agreement 0.867 and 0.839, respectively). Within-reader analysis identified subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis and supraspinatus tendon tears more frequently on the routine protocol than on Sonic DL (P 0.049 and P 0.006, respectively). CONCLUSION: Sonic DL enabled a 38.7% reduction in nominal shoulder MRI acquisition time with broadly comparable image quality and inter-reader agreement in this pilot cohort. Diagnostic equivalence was not established; subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis and supraspinatus tears were potentially less conspicuous on Sonic DL. A larger powered validation study would be needed to fully evaluate diagnostic performance.

articles.title: Underreporting of sacroiliac joint structural abnormalities on routine abdominal CT in axial spondyloarthritis: a longitudinal workflow analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To quantify documentation of predefined, conspicuous sacroiliac joint (SIJ) structural abnormalities on routine abdominal CT in patients with established axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) and identify associated factors. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective longitudinal study evaluated 516 abdominal CT examinations from 188 patients with established SpA. Two readers applied a predefined hierarchical SIJ classification, with adjudication of disagreements. The primary analysis included 226 Moderate or Major examinations; all had fusion-based patterns. Patient-clustered logistic generalized estimating equations included workflow, request-level context, structural severity, prior recognition, and scan year. RESULTS: SIJ findings were absent from 152 of 226 reports (67.3%). Total fusion was unreported in 90 of 136 examinations (66.2%), including 83 of 129 with bilateral total fusion (64.3%). Crude non-reporting was 89.2% in acute care and 50.0% in rheumatology. The four-examination MSK-oriented subgroup was combined with rheumatology for modeling. Adjusted non-reporting was 82.7% in acute care and 50.6% in the combined MSK-pathway, a 32.1-point difference (95% CI, 6.2-52.0); the corresponding OR was 0.20 (95% CI, 0.05-0.75). Structural severity and request-level context were not independently associated with non-reporting. CONCLUSION: Documentation of conspicuous SIJ structural abnormalities on routine abdominal CT was frequently absent and varied by workflow. Including a field for SIJ findings in structured abdominal CT reports may lead more radiologists to look for joint abnormalities. Automated detection requires external and prospective validation before clinical implementation.

articles.title: A transparent gel pad bolus enabling direct skin recognition in surface-guided radiation therapy.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the feasibility of repurposing a transparent ultrasound gel pad as a radiotherapy bolus, we focused on dosimetric performance and compatibility with surface-guided radiation therapy (SGRT). METHODS: A gel pad bolus composed of tamarind seed gum and polyhydric alcohols was compared with a conventional gel bolus and a thermoplastic bolus. Percent depth dose was measured for 6 MV and 10 MV photon beams and 6 MeV and 9 MeV electron beams. Straight-line optical transmittance was assessed over 380-830 nm. Surface recognition accuracy was quantified using the AlignRT SGRT system on a breast phantom. RESULTS: The gel pad produced a measurable bolus effect for both photon and electron beams, although superficial dose enhancement was lower than that of conventional materials (85.5% vs 90.3-91.5% at 6 MV). Deep doses beyond dmax agreed within 1% for photon beams. At 730 nm, the gel pad bolus demonstrated high transmittance (92.3%), compared with the gel (19.8%) and HM (36.6%) boluses. The SGRT recognition rate with the gel pad bolus (89.10%) was comparable to the no-bolus condition (92.93%, p = 0.13), whereas conventional boluses significantly reduced recognition (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: The transparent gel pad bolus enabled direct SGRT-based recognition of the underlying skin surface while maintaining clinically relevant bolus functionality. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: Optical transparency enables SGRT monitoring through a bolus, highlighting optical compatibility as an important design consideration.

articles.title: Assessment of RF-Induced Heating of Stainless-Steel Sternal Wires at 7 T MRI.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate RF-induced heating of stainless-steel sternal closures at 7 T proton MRI for simple loop and figure-of-8 configurations. METHODS: Simple loop and figure-of-8 sternal closure designs were implemented on plexiglass rods and immersed in a hydroxyethyl-cellulose phantom. Temperature was monitored by four fiber-optic sensors during RF exposure at average power levels of 3 W (conventional limit), 6 W, and 25 W for 10 min. Electromagnetic simulations were used to calculate specific absorption rate distributions, which served as input for thermal simulations. Simulated and measured temperature increases were compared at the probe locations. RESULTS: At 3 W, the maximum measured temperature increase was 0.12°C for the simple loop and 0.29°C for the figure-of-8 configuration. At 6 W, the corresponding increases were 0.38°C and 0.50°C, respectively, and at 25 W they reached 1.30°C and 2.26°C. The simple loop configuration minimally affected the simulated B1 + and SAR distributions, whereas the figure-of-8 configuration produced greater field perturbations and elevated local SAR, particularly between closely spaced wire segments. Thermal simulations reproduced the measured heating trends but consistently overestimated the measured temperature increase. CONCLUSION: RF-induced heating remained small under the investigated 7 T exposure conditions, with maximum measured temperature increases below 0.3°C for both closure configurations at the nominal operating power of 3 W. The figure-of-8 configuration produced greater electromagnetic field perturbations and heating than the simple loop configuration, indicating a more favorable RF behavior for simple loop closures.

articles.title: Whole-Ventricle Cardiac Cine MRI in a Single Breath-Hold With Slice- and Time-Dependent Deep Image Prior at 0.55T.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop a whole-ventricle cardiac cine MRI radial acquisition at 0.55T in a single breath-hold scan of approximately 12-15 s, reconstructed using a novel self-supervised slice and time-dependent deep image prior (ST-DIP) neural network. METHODS: A whole-ventricle cardiac cine MRI at 0.55T is acquired in a single breath-hold by collecting eight slices (1.5 s per slice) and reconstructing them jointly using ST-DIP. Acquisition uses a tiny golden angle radial trajectory and a balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) readout. Reconstruction uses a frequency-weighted consistency loss in the frequency domain and total variation regularization in the image domain, sharing the same network weights for all slices. The proposed approach was tested in 10 healthy subjects and was compared with time-dependent deep image prior (TD-DIP) and conventional reconstruction methods. RESULTS: ST-DIP achieves an edge sharpness of 1.15 ± 0.32  [  pixel - 1    ] at the septum, slightly higher than TD-DIP ( 1.08 ± 0.21  [  pixel - 1    ]) and significantly higher than GRASP ( 0.72 ± 0.13  [  pixel - 1    ]). The LVEF obtained with ST-DIP was 58.7 % ± 3.7 %  , comparable to the 15-s-per-slice radial reference scan ( 59.1 % ± 5.1 %  ). ST-DIP reconstructed 8 slices simultaneously in 16 ± 2   min, whereas TD-DIP, GRASP, and SENSE required sequential reconstruction times of 45 ± 4  , 12 ± 2  , and 3 min, respectively. CONCLUSION: ST-DIP enables whole-ventricle cine imaging in a single breath-hold and reconstruction of high-quality cine images at 0.55T, outperforming conventional methods in image quality while providing comparable LVEF to a 15-s-per-slice radial reference cine scan.

articles.title: FLASH effect on the liver and spleen of mice-a transcriptional perspective.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH-RT), delivered at an ultra-high dose rate (typically ≥ 40 Gy/s), has been shown to reduce normal tissue toxicity compared with conventional dose-rate radiotherapy (CONV-RT). However, the transcriptomic mechanisms underlying FLASH-mediated protection remain incompletely understood. PURPOSE: This study aimed to compare the biological effects of FLASH and CONV irradiation on mouse liver and spleen tissues and to identify molecular pathways associated with the FLASH effect from a transcriptional perspective. METHODS: C57BL/6J male mice received a single 12 Gy abdominal dose delivered at either 2 Gy/min (CONV) or 100 Gy/s (FLASH). Twelve days after irradiation, spleen and liver tissues were harvested for histological section analysis and RNA-seq. Inflammatory responses in the spleen and liver were assessed by hematoxylin-eosin staining (H&E staining) and immunohistochemical quantification. A series of bioinformatic analyses, such as gene enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis, and transcription factor prediction, were performed to explore the effect of FLASH irradiation. Subsequently, reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), western blot analysis, and immunohistochemical quantification were used to verify the bioinformatic results. RESULTS: Histological and immunohistochemical analyses showed less prominent inflammatory changes and lower immune-cell marker staining in mouse spleen and liver after FLASH than after CONV irradiation at 12 days post-irradiation. Bioinformatic analysis and corresponding experimental results revealed that compared to CONV irradiation, FLASH irradiation induced down-regulation of oxidative phosphorylation and cytoplasmic translation pathways in both mouse liver and spleen. Meanwhile, immune-related pathways, especially interferon β (IFNβ) signaling pathways, were significantly activated in both tissues after FLASH than after CONV irradiation. For these three pathways, key transcription factors were further identified and verified. Notably, STAT1 was found to play a potentially critical role in the upregulation of the IFNβ-related pathway under FLASH irradiation conditions in both liver and spleen. CONCLUSIONS: FLASH irradiation induces distinct metabolic and immune adaptations in normal mouse liver and spleen tissues compared with CONV irradiation. The coordinated suppression of metabolic and translational pathways, together with activation of IFNβ-STAT1 signaling program, provides transcriptomic evidence for potential mechanisms underlying FLASH-mediated normal tissue sparing. These findings offer candidate pathways and molecular markers for future functional validation and support the clinical translation of FLASH-RT.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence apps for medical image analysis using pyCERR and cancer genomics cloud.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To provide a software resource that enables medical researchers and practitioners to develop and apply reproducible, out-of-the-box, AI-based analysis workflows for radiological and radiotherapy data. DEVELOPMENT AND VALIDATION METHODS: The framework comprises two main components: the Python-native computational environment for radiological research (pyCERR) for radiological image processing, and the cancer genomics cloud (CGC), a National Cancer Institute-funded resource that supports cloud-hosted collaborative projects, with tools for managing collaborators and compute-hardware from providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. pyCERR is open-source (GNU GPL) and distributed at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr; it provides user-friendly data structures, simplified access to metadata across radiological imaging modalities, and tools for data transformation, AI-based image segmentation, radiomics, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI analysis, radiotherapy dose-volume histogram (DVH) feature extraction, and normal-tissue complication and tumor-control models. Radiomics features comply with the Image biomarker standardization initiative (IBSI) standards and are validated against published reference values. Unit tests covering data input/output, radiomics, DVH features, and visualization run on every code update. Workflows are containerized for reproducible, identical execution on the CGC and on local hardware. The CGC enables AI inference from radiological images to be combined with other data types such as genomics and proteomics. Our public CGC project (https://cgc.sbgenomics.com/u/sevenbridges/pycerr-radiological-radiotherapy-imageanalysis), accessible with free registration, currently includes apps for organ-at-risk (OAR) and lung-nodule segmentation based on published models trained in-house and clinically validated. These apps can be run interactively from a web browser or programmatically via a REST API with client support for multiple programming languages. Notebooks demonstrating the CGC API and pyCERR capabilities are provided at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr-notebooks. POTENTIAL APPLICATIONS: The framework facilitates end-to-end radiological image analysis and reproducible research, including data access from public and private repositories, training and inference with AI models, and utilities for data management, visualization, and simplified access to image metadata.

articles.title: Machine Learning-driven Prognostic Stratification in Metastatic Breast Cancer Using Dynamic 18F-FDG PET/CT: A Multidimensional Study Integrating Pathomics and Plasma Proteomics.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Existing baseline-dependent metastatic breast cancer (MBC) prognostic systems remain limited in capturing tumor evolution under therapeutic pressure. We aimed to develop a dynamic 18F-FDG PET/CT-derived machine learning prognostic model and systematically explore its biological rationale using pathomics and proteomics. MATERIALS AND METHODS: PET metabolic and dynamic biomarkers were extracted from serial baseline and post-treatment 18F-FDG PET/CT images of 112 retrospectively included MBC patients. Independent prognostic biomarkers were identified using Cox regression. Prognostic models were constructed through multiple machine learning algorithms, with interpretability provided by SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Pathomics (n = 45) and plasma proteomics (n = 48) analyses were performed to characterize risk-associated biological features. RESULTS: Post-treatment metabolic (SUVmax2) and dynamic (ΔSULmax) PET biomarkers emerged as independent prognostic factors for progression-free survival. The final random survival forest model, termed the dynamic PET/CT-based MBC (dPMBC) prognostic model, achieved favorable prognostic stratification, yielding area under the curve values of 0.881 and 0.807 in the training and testing cohorts, respectively. SHAP identified SUVmax2 as the most influential predictive feature. Pathomics revealed distinct morphological evolution in high-risk patients, characterized by extracellular matrix remodeling and nuclear atypia. Plasma proteomics highlighted GART-centric metabolic reprogramming and immune-related alterations involving HLA-C and STAT1 within this high-risk group. CONCLUSION: The dPMBC prognostic model, integrating dynamic PET biomarkers, demonstrates promising predictive performance and biological interpretability. It enables early identification of high-risk patients during first-line therapy, supporting closer monitoring and timely individualized treatment adjustment. Pathomics and proteomics further provide biological insights into PET/CT-derived risk stratification in MBC.

Rapid On-Site Evaluation in Ultrasound-Guided Fine-Needle Aspiration Biopsy of Parotid Gland Lesions: A Decade of Experience.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate the contribution of rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) to the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) in parotid gland lesions. METHODS: In this single-center retrospective study, 589 parotid gland lesions evaluated between January 2012 and September 2022 were included. All procedures were performed under ultrasound guidance by interventional radiologists with more than 15 years of experience, using 20-gauge fine-needle aspiration needles. ROSE was performed by a cytopathologist with more than 20 years of experience. Cytological results were classified as diagnostic, suspicious, indeterminate, or non-diagnostic. For patients who underwent surgery, postoperative histopathological diagnoses were compared with cytopathological findings. RESULTS: Among 589 lesions, 504 (85.6%) were benign and 85 (14.4%) were malignant. The most common benign lesions were Warthin tumor (33.6%) and pleomorphic adenoma (26.1%). FNAB results were diagnostic in 541 lesions (91.9%), suspicious in 38 (6.5%), indeterminate in 8 (1.4%), and non-diagnostic in only 2 (0.3%). Among the 284 patients who underwent surgical resection, ROSE-guided FNAB cytology was concordant with postoperative histopathology in 278 (97.9%). CONCLUSION: ROSE-guided FNAB represents a highly accurate, minimally invasive diagnostic strategy for parotid gland lesions, yielding definitive cytological results in a single procedure while substantially reducing the need for repeat sampling or more invasive diagnostic approaches.

articles.title: Value of Multimodal Ultrasound Imaging With Super-Resolution in the Differential Diagnosis of Benign and Malignant Superficial Lymph Nodes: A Dual-Center Prospective Study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Accurate differential diagnosis of benign and malignant superficial lymph nodes (LNs) is critical for clinical management. The objectives of this study were to explore the feasibility and clinical value of super-resolution ultrasound (SRUS) in the differential diagnosis of superficial lymphadenopathy and to establish and validate a multimodal ultrasound diagnostic model based on conventional ultrasound (US), contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), and SRUS, so as to improve the accuracy of distinguishing benign from malignant superficial LNs in clinical practice. METHODS: A total of 200 LNs from 165 patients with superficial lymphadenectasis were prospectively enrolled from two medical centers. All patients underwent conventional US, CEUS, and SRUS imaging. Predictive models were constructed based on the conventional US, CEUS, and SRUS features in the training cohort, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity were calculated to evaluate their predictive performance in the external validation cohort. RESULTS: The training cohort comprised 117 patients with a total of 140 LNs including 46 benign and 94 malignant lesions. The validation cohort included 48 patients with 60 LNs in total, with 21 benign and 39 malignant lesions. Among the models constructed based on the training cohort, the SRUS model exhibited significantly superior diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.822) to the conventional US and CEUS models (P < .05). The combined model, integrating all three modalities, achieved an AUC of 0.892 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.833-0.952) in the training cohort and 0.890 (95% CI: 0.791-0.990) in the external validation cohort, demonstrating excellent and stable diagnostic performance. CONCLUSION: SRUS provides crucial imaging evidence for the non-invasive qualitative evaluation of LNs. The multimodal diagnostic model incorporating the features of US, CEUS, and SRUS can significantly improve the accuracy of distinguishing benign from malignant LNs.

Association of Transabdominal Ultrasound Evaluation of Pelvic Free Fluid Presence, Depth, Morphology, and Location with Pathology in Reproductive-Aged Females Presenting to the Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the association between nontraumatic pelvic free fluid (PFF) characteristics (presence, depth, morphology, and location) and pathology in reproductive-aged females presenting to the emergency department (ED). METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of patients aged 18-40 years with a uterus who were non-pregnant or in their first trimester of pregnancy and underwent pelvic ultrasound from January 1, 2020 to December 31, 2024. Exclusion criteria were bilateral oophorectomy, known ascites, recent trauma or abdominal surgery, concurrent reproductive endocrinology treatment, or inadequate ultrasound images. The primary outcome was pathology based on a composite clinical reference standard. Two blinded, ultrasound-trained emergency physicians reviewed point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) images for PFF presence, morphology (stripe, small pocket, large pocket, sliver), location, and maximal depth. Multivariable regression analyses evaluated associations between PFF characteristics and pathology. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis determined optimal depth thresholds for predicting pathology. RESULTS: Of 746 pelvic ultrasound examinations, 672 patients were included. Pathology was identified in 126 of 672 (18.8%) patients and PFF was present in 174/672 (25.9%). PFF was associated with pathology (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.0; 95% CI 2.0-4.6). A 6.9-mm threshold demonstrated modest discrimination for pathology (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.69); mean PFF depth was 9.5 ± 7.8 mm. Stripe morphology, observed in 54 of 174 (31.0%) patients with PFF, was associated with increased odds of pathology compared with other morphologies (aOR 3.6; 95% CI 1.8-7.3; p < .001). Anteriorly located fluid relative to the uterus was associated with gynecologic pathology (aOR 3.4, 95% CI 1.2-9.4). CONCLUSION: PFF characteristics on PoCUS may help refine diagnostic prioritization for pathology in reproductive-aged females presenting to the ED.

articles.title: Mitigating errors in musculoskeletal radiology: a multilevel framework.
articles.abstract: Reporting errors are an unavoidable reality for any active, practicing radiologist. However, they can be minimised through open discussion, meticulous training, and openness to feedback. In an era marked by escalating imaging volumes, complex caseloads, and systemic workforce burnout, achieving an error-free practice is a statistical impossibility; baseline radiological error rates are estimated in the literature to range between 3% and 5% for decades. However, this reality should not deter radiologists from pursuing continuous diagnostic refinement. This article explores the intricate cognitive and perceptual pitfalls that lead to interpretive misses in musculoskeletal (MSK) radiology reporting, such as satisfaction of search, anchoring bias, framing bias, and the misinterpretation of common anatomical variants or technical artefacts (like the magic angle effect). Utilising illustrated case examples to highlight these common blind spots, the review transitions from identifying diagnostic errors to outlining actionable, multi-tiered strategies for mitigation. At the individual level, it emphasises checklist utility and historical image comparison. At the departmental level, it advocates for a shift from blame-free frameworks toward a 'just culture' via Radiology Events and Learning Meetings (REALM), while directly addressing the detrimental impact of medical incivility on psychological safety. Finally, at the international level, it examines the integration of artificial intelligence as a collaborative second reader. This review helps radiologists transform interpretive errors into shared clinical knowledge, with the aim of reducing or minimising errors and ultimately promoting patient safety in a psychologically safe environment.

articles.title: A deep learning radiomics model based on multiparametric MRI for predicting the efficacy of neoadjuvant chemotherapy in axillary lymph nodes of breast cancer.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: In this study, we developed and validated a deep learning radiomics clinical (DLRC) model integrating multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and clinical data to predict axillary pathological complete response (apCR) in cN+ breast cancer patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively collected data from 221 eligible breast cancer patients. The DLRC model integrated radiomics features and deep learning scores (DL-Scores) derived from mpMRI, together with clinical risk factors, to predict apCR. Seven classifiers were employed for model construction, and the optimal classifier was selected based on classification performance to build the final model. Model performance was evaluated using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, area under the curve (AUC), calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Classification performance was assessed via the confusion matrix. Additionally, SHAP plots were utilized for interpretability analysis of the model. RESULTS: Multivariate analysis confirmed that progesterone receptor (PR), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), clinical T stage (OR = 0.258), and time-intensity curve (TIC) were significantly associated with apCR. The mpMRI based DLRC model achieved AUCs of 0.949 (95% CI, 0.912-0.986) and 0.932 (95% CI, 0.867-0.998) in the training and validation sets. SHAP analysis further revealed the interpretability of the model. The confusion matrix visually demonstrated the consistency between the predicted results and the true labels, validating the classification performance of the model. CONCLUSION: The DLRC model effectively predicts apCR in breast cancer patients after NAC. It can serve as an auxiliary tool for clinicians in identifying potential candidates for axillary de-escalation, offering support for personalized precision treatment. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD-AI reporting checklist.

articles.title: Endovascular management of arteriovenous fistula postbiopsy of pediatric transplanted kidney using embolization with detachable coils.
articles.abstract: AIM: Ultrasound (US)-guided transplant kidney biopsy is required to exclude rejection or other causes of allograft dysfunction. Arteriovenous fistula (AVF) is a known complication, with occurrence rates from 1.5% to 18%. AVF may heal spontaneously; however, persistent lesions may result in hypertension, renal impairment, or hematuria. The purpose of the present study was to investigate the technical details and outcomes of postbiopsy kidney transplant AVF in children, treated by interventional radiology. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a retrospective review (2019-2026) of renal transplant AVF embolization procedures in a pediatric tertiary care center. Clinical details, including transplant history, biopsy, AVF diagnosis, embolization procedural details, and postembolization clinical course, were collected. Technical success was defined as occlusion of the lesion with cessation of early venous filling, and improved flow to the adjacent parenchyma. RESULTS: Four cases were identified, with a mean age of 15 years 1 month. Embolization was indicated due to long-term persistence and increasing lesion size on serial imaging. US and computed tomography (CT) were used for procedural planning. In all cases, a femoral arterial access approach was used, with a combination of two detachable coils (anchoring and packing), obtaining AVF occlusion. A 100% technical success rate was achieved. This has persisted in postprocedure imaging follow-up (mean follow-up: 17 months [2-36]). No minor or major adverse events were observed. CONCLUSION: This study illustrates that embolization with detachable coils is a viable option to treat postbiopsy kidney transplant AVF in children. An anchoring and packing coil combination was feasible and effective in this small cohort.

articles.title: Misreporting of study design and validation status in a study of early tumour shrinkage in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
articles.abstract: This letter to the Editor addresses a fundamental inconsistency in the reporting of study design and validation status in the article by Zhou et al. published in Cancer Imaging. The authors state in the Methods section that the study retrospectively analyzed 125 patients, yet the Introduction and Discussion claim that the study prospectively validated the prognostic value of early tumour shrinkage (ETS) and depth of response (DoR). Prospective validation requires a priori model specification and evaluation on subsequently collected data, whereas retrospective analyses are inherently susceptible to selection bias and cannot establish prospective validity. The authors also conclude that they developed and validated a comprehensive predictive model, but no external validation, temporal validation, or clearly described internal validation procedure is reported. The ETS and DoR thresholds were derived from ROC analysis within the same cohort and then applied to the same patients for survival analysis, risking overfitting and optimistic bias. Additionally, the Results report "responders (n = 109) and non-responders (n = 12)," while the corresponding results in the original article by Zhou et al. [1] list the ratio as 12/109, reversing the group labels. We respectfully suggest that the authors clarify the actual study design, remove any claim of prospective validation if the study is retrospective, provide evidence of validation or remove the claim of a validated model, and correct the numerical inconsistency. Such corrections would uphold the scientific integrity of the literature.
